mark is allowed and ignored. A byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 is
error RP0005.

**[lexical.source.charset]** Outside comments, pragmas and `"..."` (WSTRING)
literals, only ASCII characters may appear. Any other character there is
error RP0005.

**[lexical.whitespace]** Whitespace is space (U+0020), tab (U+0009), line feed
(U+000A), carriage return (U+000D) and form feed (U+000C). Whitespace
separates tokens and has no other meaning. A line ends at LF or CR LF.

**[lexical.longest-match]** The lexer always takes the longest sequence of
characters that forms a valid token. For example, `<=` is one token, and
`1..10` is the tokens `1`, `..`, `10`.

## 2. Comments

**[lexical.comment.block]** `(*` starts a comment that ends at the next `*)`.

**[lexical.comment.cblock]** `/*` starts a comment that ends at the next `*/`.

**[lexical.comment.line]** `//` starts a comment that ends at the end of the line.

**[lexical.comment.nesting]** Comments do not nest. An opener of the same
kind inside a block comment (`(*` inside `(* *)`, or `/*` inside `/* */`) is
warning RP0003, and the comment still ends at the first closer.

**[lexical.comment.unterminated]** A block comment with no closer before end
of file is error RP0001, reported at the opener.

Comment openers inside string literals and pragmas are not comments.

## 3. Identifiers

**[lexical.identifier]** An identifier starts with an ASCII letter or `_`,
followed by any number of ASCII letters, digits and `_`. All characters are
significant; there is no length limit.

**[lexical.identifier.case]** Identifiers and keywords are case-insensitive.
They are compared after ASCII lower-case folding. `Motor_On`, `MOTOR_ON` and
`motor_on` are the same name. Tools keep the spelling of the declaration
when they print a name.

**[lexical.identifier.underscore]** Two or more consecutive underscores in an
identifier are warning RP0006. (Ed2 forbade them; CODESYS accepts them, so
RootPLC accepts them with a warning to keep migrated code compiling.)

**[lexical.keyword]** The keywords below are reserved. Using one as an
identifier is error RP0004.

```
ABSTRACT ACTION AND AND_THEN ARRAY AT BY CASE CLASS CONFIGURATION CONSTANT
CONTINUE DO ELSE ELSIF END_ACTION END_CASE END_CLASS END_CONFIGURATION
END_FOR END_FUNCTION END_FUNCTION_BLOCK END_IF END_INTERFACE END_METHOD
END_NAMESPACE END_PROGRAM END_REPEAT END_RESOURCE END_STEP END_STRUCT
END_TEST END_TRANSITION END_TYPE END_VAR END_WHILE EXIT EXTENDS FALSE FINAL
FOR FROM FUNCTION FUNCTION_BLOCK IF IMPLEMENTS INITIAL_STEP INTERFACE
INTERNAL METHOD MOD NAMESPACE NON_RETAIN NOT NULL OF ON OR OR_ELSE OVERLAP
OVERRIDE PRIVATE PROGRAM PROTECTED PUBLIC READ_ONLY READ_WRITE REF REF_TO
REPEAT RESOURCE RETAIN RETURN STEP STRUCT SUPER TASK TEST THEN THIS TO
TRANSITION TRUE TYPE UNTIL USING VAR VAR_ACCESS VAR_CONFIG VAR_EXTERNAL
VAR_GLOBAL VAR_INPUT VAR_IN_OUT VAR_OUTPUT VAR_STAT VAR_TEMP WHILE WITH XOR
```

Elementary type names (spec/02-types.md) are also reserved.

**[lexical.keywords.soft]** `AT`, `ON`, `STEP`, `TASK`, `TRANSITION`,
`INITIAL_STEP`, `WITH` and `OVERRIDE` start constructs only in a few places
(a located variable, a configuration, SFC, which RootPLC does not parse, a
method modifier), and CODESYS and TwinCAT code uses them as ordinary names. RootPLC reads them as names
everywhere else; declaring one as a name is warning RP0124 instead of
RP0004. A member or enumeration value may also be called `NULL` or `REF`
(warning RP0124); it is then written after a `.` (`E_State.NULL`, `x.Ref`),
where any keyword is read as a member name.

## 4. Numeric literals

**[lexical.literal.integer]** A decimal integer literal is a sequence of
digits. A based literal is `2#`, `8#` or `16#` followed by digits of that
base; hex digits are case-insensitive (`16#ff` = `16#FF`). A digit that is
not valid for the base is error RP0008.

**[lexical.literal.underscore]** A single `_` may appear between two digits of
any numeric literal and is ignored (`1_000_000`, `2#1010_0101`). An
underscore at the start or end of the digits, next to `#` or `.`, or doubled,
is error RP0007.

**[lexical.literal.sign]** A literal has no sign. A leading `-` or `+` is the
unary operator. Constant folding makes `-128` valid where a SINT is expected
(spec/02-types.md [types.literal.range]).

**[lexical.literal.real]** A real literal is `digits . digits`, optionally
followed by an exponent `E` or `e`, an optional sign, and digits. Both sides
of the point are required: `1.` and `.5` are error RP0008. A literal with an
exponent but no point, such as `1E-6`, is accepted as a real with warning
RP0017: IEC 61131-3 requires the point, but CODESYS and TwinCAT accept this
form and real code uses it. The portable spelling is `1.0E-6`.

**[lexical.literal.typed]** A typed literal is an elementary type name, `#`,
and a literal: `INT#5`, `REAL#1.5`, `BYTE#16#FF`, `BOOL#1`. An unknown type
name before `#` is error RP0014. For enumerations, `Type#Value` names an
enumeration value (spec/02-types.md).

**[lexical.literal.bool]** `TRUE` and `FALSE` are the boolean literals.
`BOOL#0` and `BOOL#1` are also accepted.

## 5. Character and string literals

**[lexical.literal.string]** `'...'` is a STRING literal and `"..."` is a
WSTRING literal. A literal cannot contain a raw line end; a literal not
closed before the end of the line is error RP0002.

**[lexical.literal.string.latin1]** A STRING literal may contain only
characters U+0000–U+00FF, stored as one byte each (Latin-1). Any other
character is error RP0009 with the hint to use a WSTRING literal. WSTRING
is UTF-16.

**[lexical.literal.escape]** `$` starts an escape sequence. Letters are
case-insensitive.

| Escape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$$` | `$` |
| `$'` | `'` (in STRING; in WSTRING also allowed) |
| `$"` | `"` (in WSTRING; in STRING also allowed) |
| `$L` or `$N` | line feed |
| `$P` | form feed |
| `$R` | carriage return |
| `$T` | tab |
| `$hh` | byte with hex value hh (STRING only) |
| `$hhhh` | UTF-16 code unit hhhh (WSTRING only) |

Any other character after `$` is error RP0010. A bare `'` inside a STRING
literal ends the literal; likewise `"` inside a WSTRING literal.

**[lexical.literal.char]** `CHAR#'a'` and `WCHAR#"a"` are character literals.
The quoted part must contain exactly one character or escape sequence;
otherwise error RP0008.

## 6. Duration and date/time literals

**[lexical.literal.duration]** A duration literal is a prefix `T#`, `TIME#`,
`LT#` or `LTIME#`, an optional `-`, and one or more fields. Each field is a
number followed by a unit: `d`, `h`, `m`, `s`, `ms`, `us`, `ns`. Prefixes and
units are case-insensitive, and `_` may separate fields (`T#1h_30m`).

- Units appear in descending order, each at most once.
- Only the last field may have a fraction (`T#1.5s`).
- Only the first field may exceed its natural range (`T#90m`). CODESYS and
  TwinCAT also accept a later field out of range (`T#1h90m`, the fields are
  added): warning RP0128.

A literal that breaks any other of these is error RP0011.

**[lexical.literal.date]** Date and time literals:

| Prefix | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `D#`, `DATE#`, `LD#`, `LDATE#` | `yyyy-mm-dd` | `D#2026-11-03` |
| `TOD#`, `TIME_OF_DAY#`, `LTOD#`, `LTIME_OF_DAY#` | `hh:mm:ss[.f]` | `TOD#14:30:00.5` |
| `DT#`, `DATE_AND_TIME#`, `LDT#`, `LDATE_AND_TIME#` | `yyyy-mm-dd-hh:mm:ss[.f]` | `DT#2026-11-03-14:30:00` |

The seconds may be left out (`TOD#12:00`, CODESYS and TwinCAT); they are
then 0, with warning RP0133 ([scope.vendor-forms]). A value outside the calendar or clock (month 13, 30 February, hour
24) is error RP0012. A malformed literal is error RP0011.

## 7. Pragmas

**[lexical.pragma]** `{` starts a pragma that ends at the next `}`. Pragmas do
not nest. The first word names the pragma. Pragmas that RootPLC defines are
listed in spec/09-properties.md; for example `{attribute 'name'}`. An unknown
pragma is warning RP0013 and is otherwise ignored. A pragma with no closing
`}` before end of file is error RP0015.

## 7a. Directly represented variables

**[lexical.direct-variable]** `%` followed by a location `I` (input), `Q`
(output) or `M` (memory), an optional size `X` (bit), `B`, `W`, `D` or `L`,
and an address: digits separated by single dots (`%IX0.0`, `%QW4`, `%MD12`),
or `*` for an address assigned later in the configuration (`%I*`). Letters
are case-insensitive. Anything else after `%` is error RP0016.

## 8. Operators and punctuation

**[lexical.punctuation]** The punctuation tokens are:

```
:=  =>  ?=  (  )  [  ]  ,  ;  :  .  ..  #  ^
+  -  *  /  **  &  =  <>  <  >  <=  >=
```

`AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `NOT`, `MOD`, `AND_THEN` and `OR_ELSE` are keyword
operators. Any other character outside a token, comment, literal or pragma
is error RP0005.

## Open questions

- Nested comments: check whether CODESYS supports nesting of `(* *)` by
  default. If it does, consider supporting nesting for migration.
- `?=` (assignment attempt, Ed3) is reserved as a token; its semantics belong
  in spec/05-statements.md.


======== Specification: spec/02-types.md ========

# Data types

*Status: draft v0.1. Normative. Diagnostic range RP0100–RP0199.*

This chapter defines the data types, their values and the conversions
between them. Where IEC 61131-3 Ed3 leaves a choice to the implementation,
RootPLC fixes it, so that the VM, generated C and CBMC all agree bit for bit.

## 1. Elementary types

**[types.elementary]** The elementary types are:

| Type | Size | Values / representation | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BOOL` | 1 byte | `FALSE`, `TRUE` | `FALSE` |
| `SINT` / `USINT` | 8 bit | signed / unsigned two's complement | `0` |
| `INT` / `UINT` | 16 bit | " | `0` |
| `DINT` / `UDINT` | 32 bit | " | `0` |
| `LINT` / `ULINT` | 64 bit | " | `0` |
| `REAL` | 32 bit | IEEE 754 binary32 | `0.0` |
| `LREAL` | 64 bit | IEEE 754 binary64 | `0.0` |
| `BYTE` / `WORD` / `DWORD` / `LWORD` | 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 bit | bit string | `0` |
| `TIME` | 32 bit | signed milliseconds | `T#0s` |
| `LTIME` | 64 bit | signed nanoseconds | `LT#0s` |
| `DATE` | 32 bit | seconds since 1970-01-01, day-aligned | `D#1970-01-01` |
| `TIME_OF_DAY` (`TOD`) | 32 bit | milliseconds since midnight | `TOD#00:00:00` |
| `DATE_AND_TIME` (`DT`) | 32 bit | seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 | `DT#1970-01-01-00:00:00` |
| `LDATE`, `LTOD`, `LDT` | 64 bit | nanoseconds since the same origins | origin |
| `CHAR` / `WCHAR` | 8 / 16 bit | Latin-1 byte / UTF-16 code unit | `'$00'` |
| `STRING[n]` | n+1 bytes | Latin-1, default n = 80 | `''` |
| `WSTRING[n]` | 2(n+1) bytes | UTF-16, default n = 80 | `""` |

The 32-bit `TIME`, `DATE`, `TOD` and `DT` follow CODESYS, so that migrated
programs keep their behaviour. New code should prefer the `L` types.

**[types.default-init]** A variable without an initial value starts with the
default of its type. Elements of arrays and members of structures get the
default of their own type, unless the type declaration gives one.

## 2. Arithmetic semantics

**[types.time.arith]** `+` and `-` combine times and durations as IEC 61131-3
ed.3 defines them: `TOD ± TIME` gives `TOD`, `DT ± TIME` gives `DT`, and
`TOD - TOD`, `DT - DT` and `DATE - DATE` give `TIME`; with the 64-bit types
`LTOD ± LTIME`, `LDT ± LTIME` and `LTOD - LTOD`, `LDT - LDT`, `LDATE - LDATE`
(the result `LTIME`). A time of day wraps around midnight. `DT ± TIME` keeps
whole seconds (the milliseconds of the duration are dropped, towards zero).
Other combinations of time types are RP0103.

**[types.int.overflow]** Integer arithmetic at run time wraps around in two's
complement (for example, `SINT#127 + 1` gives `-128`). Overflow while
evaluating a constant expression at compile time is error RP0101.

**[types.int.division]** Integer division truncates toward zero. The result
of `MOD` has the sign of the dividend. Division or `MOD` by zero at run time
raises the runtime fault `DIV_BY_ZERO` (spec/06-tasks-config.md); with a
constant divisor of zero it is error RP0101.

**[types.real]** `REAL` and `LREAL` follow IEEE 754 with round-to-nearest-even.
Infinities and NaN are ordinary values and never raise a fault.

## 3. Literals and types

**[types.literal.range]** A literal, or a constant expression, must fit the
type it is used as. `SINT#200` or `x : SINT := 200` is error RP0102.
`-128` fits SINT because the minus is folded first.

**[types.literal.untyped]** An untyped literal takes its type from its
context: the variable assigned, the parameter passed, or the other operand.
With no context, an integer literal is `DINT` if it fits and `LINT`
otherwise, and a real literal is `LREAL`.

## 4. Conversions

**[types.conversion.implicit]** A value converts implicitly only when no
value is lost. The allowed implicit conversions are (transitively):

| From | To |
|---|---|
| `SINT` | `INT`, `DINT`, `LINT`, `REAL`, `LREAL` |
| `INT` | `DINT`, `LINT`, `REAL`, `LREAL` |
| `DINT` | `LINT`, `LREAL` |
| `USINT` | `UINT`, `UDINT`, `ULINT`, `INT`, `DINT`, `LINT`, `REAL`, `LREAL` |
| `UINT` | `UDINT`, `ULINT`, `DINT`, `LINT`, `REAL`, `LREAL` |
| `UDINT` | `ULINT`, `LINT`, `LREAL` |
| `REAL` | `LREAL` |
| `BOOL` | `BYTE` |
| `BYTE` → `WORD` → `DWORD` → `LWORD` | each wider bit string |
| `TIME` | `LTIME` |
| `DATE`, `TOD`, `DT` | `LDATE`, `LTOD`, `LDT` respectively |
| `CHAR` | `STRING` |
| `WCHAR` | `WSTRING` |

Every other conversion, including narrowing, signed to unsigned, integer to
`BOOL`, integer to bit string, enumeration to integer and `STRING` to
`WSTRING`, is error RP0103. The fix hint names the explicit function.

**[types.conversion.explicit]** Explicit conversions are written
`<FROM>_TO_<TO>(x)` (for example `INT_TO_SINT`) or the overloaded `TO_<TO>(x)`.
Their results are fully defined:

- integer to integer: the value modulo 2^n, read as the target type (wrap);
- real to integer: round to nearest, ties away from zero; saturate at the
  target limits; NaN gives 0. `TRUNC` rounds toward zero instead;
- integer to real: round to nearest-even;
- bit string to integer and back: the same bits, with the target width;
- to `STRING` / `WSTRING`: the text form. Integers and bit strings are
  written in decimal, `BOOL` as `TRUE` / `FALSE`, reals in the shortest
  decimal form that reads back as the same value of their own type (`REAL`
  0.1 is `0.1`), whole numbers with `.0` (`1.0`) and very large or small
  magnitudes (from 1E16, below 1E-5) in exponent form without `+`
  (`-3.402823E38`, `1E-7`); `TIME` and `LTIME` as literals in their largest
  units with zero units left out (`T#49d17h2m47s295ms`, `T#1s500ms`,
  `T#0ms`, `LT#1ms500us`), as TwinCAT writes them; and `DATE`, `TOD`, `DT` and their `L` forms as
  literals: `D#2017-04-04`, `TOD#12:42:42.5`, `DT#2017-04-04-12:42:42`
  (fractions of a second only when not zero). `CHAR` / `WCHAR` give the
  one-character string.

## 5. Generic types

**[types.generic]** The generic types group elementary types:

```
ANY
├─ ANY_DERIVED
└─ ANY_ELEMENTARY
   ├─ ANY_MAGNITUDE
   │  ├─ ANY_NUM
   │  │  ├─ ANY_REAL      REAL, LREAL
   │  │  └─ ANY_INT
   │  │     ├─ ANY_SIGNED    SINT, INT, DINT, LINT
   │  │     └─ ANY_UNSIGNED  USINT, UINT, UDINT, ULINT
   │  └─ ANY_DURATION   TIME, LTIME
   ├─ ANY_BIT          BOOL, BYTE, WORD, DWORD, LWORD
   ├─ ANY_CHARS
   │  ├─ ANY_STRING    STRING, WSTRING
   │  └─ ANY_CHAR      CHAR, WCHAR
   └─ ANY_DATE         DATE, TOD, DT, LDATE, LTOD, LDT
```

Generic types may appear only in the signatures of standard-library
functions. Using one in a user declaration is error RP0104.

## 6. Derived types

Derived types are declared between `TYPE` and `END_TYPE`. Referring to a
type that is not declared is error RP0111.

**[types.derived.alias]** `TYPE Speed : INT := 10; END_TYPE` declares an alias
with an optional new default. An alias of an elementary type is compatible
with its base type in both directions.

**[types.equivalence]** Apart from aliases of elementary types, types are
compatible by name only. Two structures with identical members but
different names are different types.

**[types.derived.subrange]** `TYPE Percent : INT (0..100); END_TYPE`. The
bounds are constant and lower <= upper (otherwise RP0108). The default is the
lower bound. A constant outside the range is error RP0105. A run-time
assignment outside the range raises the fault `RANGE` in the VM and
simulator; in generated C the check can be switched off per build.

**[types.derived.enum]** `TYPE Mode : (Off, Manual, Auto); END_TYPE`, or with
a base type and values: `TYPE Mode : INT (Off := 0, Auto := 10); END_TYPE`.
Without explicit values the base type is `INT` and the values are 0, 1, 2...
in order. The CODESYS and TwinCAT spelling with the base type after the
values, `(Off := 0, Auto := 10) UINT`, means the same and is accepted with
warning RP0115. The default is the first value. `Mode#Auto` names a value; plain `Auto` is
allowed when exactly one enumeration in scope has it. When several have it,
the enumeration the context expects decides, as in CODESYS and TwinCAT: the
target of an assignment, the other operand of a comparison, the CASE
selector, the parameter of a call or the variable being initialised;
without such a context it is error RP0106.
The CODESYS and TwinCAT spelling `Mode.Auto` (also qualified by a namespace,
`NS.Mode.Auto`) means `Mode#Auto` and is accepted with warning RP0122 when
`Mode` is not the name of a variable, also as a CASE label.
Enumerations do not convert implicitly to integers (RP0103); use `TO_INT`,
except as [types.derived.enum.integer] allows.

**[types.derived.enum.integer]** CODESYS and TwinCAT let enumeration values
stand for their integers; RootPLC accepts this with warning RP0129. An
enumeration value converts implicitly to an integer or bit-string type, and
in a comparison with an integer or with a value of another enumeration both
sides are compared as integers. Unless the enumeration is declared with
`{attribute 'strict'}` before its name, an integer (or a value of another
enumeration) may also be assigned to an enumeration variable and arithmetic
on enumeration values gives a result of the base type; with the attribute
these stay RP0103, except that a constant equal to one of the type's values
may be assigned. The value is not checked against the enumeration's values.

**[types.derived.struct]** `STRUCT ... END_STRUCT` declares members with
optional initial values; IEC 61131-3 requires at least one member, and an
empty structure (CODESYS, TwinCAT) is warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]). A structure that contains itself, directly or
through other structures or arrays, is error RP0107. (`REF_TO` to itself is
allowed.) `TYPE B EXTENDS A : STRUCT … END_STRUCT` (CODESYS and TwinCAT, warning
RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms])) gives
B the members of A first, with A's initial values, then its own; the base
must be a structure (RP0111).

**[types.conversion.vendor]** CODESYS and TwinCAT accept some mixes that
IEC 61131-3 rejects; RootPLC accepts them with a warning: arithmetic on bit
strings (`dw + 1`), bitwise operators on integers (`n AND 16#FF`) and bit
strings as array indexes (`a[b]` with `b : BYTE`), and an unsigned integer
mixed with or assigned to a bit string of the same size (`UDINT` and
`DWORD`) are warning RP0126; the
integer literals `0` and `1` as `BOOL` and `0` as a reference (`NULL`) are
warning RP0127.

**[types.derived.union]** `UNION ... END_UNION` (CODESYS and TwinCAT, warning
RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms])) declares
members that share one storage area; it is checked like a structure and its
size (`SIZEOF`) is that of its largest member, rounded to its alignment. The
VM does not model shared storage yet: accessing a member while running stops
with the fault `UNSUPPORTED`.

**[types.derived.array]** `ARRAY[l1..u1, l2..u2] OF T`. Bounds are constant
`DINT` expressions with l <= u, otherwise error RP0108. A constant index
outside the bounds is error RP0109. A run-time index outside the bounds
raises the fault `INDEX`. `ARRAY[*]` is allowed only for `VAR_IN_OUT`
parameters. IEC 61131-3 indexes only arrays; indexing a value that is
not an array, a string or a reference is error RP0103. CODESYS and TwinCAT
also index strings: `s[i]` is the code of character i counted from 0, a
`BYTE` for `STRING` and a `WORD` for `WSTRING`; it reads 0 at and after the
end of the string, and an index above the declared length is the fault
`INDEX`. Assigning `s[i]` replaces character i, appends one when i is the
current length, and cuts the string there when the value is 0; an index at
or above the declared length is the fault `INDEX`. RootPLC accepts this with
warning RP0135 ([scope.vendor-forms]).

**[types.derived.string]** `STRING[n]` and `WSTRING[n]` with 1 <= n <= 65535
(otherwise RP0108). The CODESYS and TwinCAT spelling `STRING(n)` means the
same and is accepted with warning RP0112, because real code uses it widely;
the portable spelling is `STRING[n]`. Assigning a longer string truncates it to n characters.
A string literal longer than n in a declaration or constant assignment is
warning RP0110.

**[types.reference]** `REF_TO T` is a reference to a variable of type T.
`REF(x)` takes a reference, `r^` dereferences it, and `NULL` is the empty
reference. Dereferencing `NULL` raises the fault `NULL_REF`. CODESYS
`POINTER TO T` is read as `REF_TO T` with warning RP0116, and `ADR(x)` as
`REF(x)` with warning RP0117; pointer arithmetic is not supported (an
arithmetic operator on a reference is RP0103). The CODESYS / TwinCAT index
on a pointer, `p[i]`, is accepted with warning RP0135: it is the element i
places after the target, which must lie inside the same array (or
structure) and hold a value of the same kind; otherwise the fault `INDEX`.
`p[0]` is the target itself. `POINTER TO` is not part of
the language.

**[types.reference.alias]** CODESYS `REFERENCE TO T` declares an alias,
accepted with warning RP0118: the variable holds a reference, but every use
of it reads or writes the target. `r REF= x` makes `r` refer to `x`, and
`__ISVALIDREF(r)` is TRUE when `r` refers to something. Using an alias that
refers to nothing is the fault `NULL_REF`. The importer maps it to `REF_TO`
where it can and reports the rest.


======== Specification: spec/03-variables.md ========

# Variables and declarations

*Status: draft v0.1 (syntax). Normative. Diagnostic range RP0200–RP0299 (shared with 04).*

This chapter defines how variables are declared and how names are resolved.
Retain behaviour follows in a later revision.
Grammar notation: `[x]` optional, `{x}` zero or more, `|` alternative,
`'…'` a literal token.

**[variables.section]** Declarations are grouped in sections:

```
var_section  = section_kw { 'CONSTANT' | 'RETAIN' | 'NON_RETAIN' | access | 'PERSISTENT' } { var_decl } 'END_VAR'
access       = 'PUBLIC' | 'PRIVATE' | 'PROTECTED' | 'INTERNAL'
section_kw   = 'VAR' | 'VAR_INPUT' | 'VAR_OUTPUT' | 'VAR_IN_OUT' | 'VAR_TEMP'
             | 'VAR_STAT' | 'VAR_GLOBAL' | 'VAR_EXTERNAL'
```

A POU may contain any number of sections, in any order, before its body.
Access specifiers (IEC 61131-3 ed.3) are accepted, and TwinCAT `PERSISTENT`
with warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]).
Variables of a `VAR PUBLIC` section can be read and written from outside the
block, like inputs; other access checks and persistence follow in a later
revision.

**[variables.static]** Variables of a `VAR_STAT` section (CODESYS and
TwinCAT) exist once per function block, program or method, not once per
instance: every instance reads and writes the same variable, and its initial
value is set once, before any instance's FB_init. A variable a block
inherits belongs to the block that declares it. Whether IEC 61131-3 defines
`VAR_STAT` is not yet checked against the standard's text, so it carries no
portability warning for now ([scope.iec]).

**[variables.declaration]** A declaration names one or more variables of one
type, with an optional initial value, and ends with `;`:

```
var_decl     = name { ',' name } [ 'AT' direct_variable ] ':' type_spec [ ':=' initializer ] ';'
```

A keyword or elementary type name used as `name` is error RP0004
([lexical.keyword]). A missing `;` is error RP0301 ([statements.terminator]).

**[variables.constant-names]** A variable of a `VAR CONSTANT` section whose
initial value is a constant expression is itself a constant: initial values
and array bounds of the same POU may name it, declared before or after them
(`current : INT := EMPTY;`, `ARRAY[0..LAST] OF INT`). An array bound must be
a constant expression RootPLC can evaluate: a literal, such a constant, a
global constant (also qualified, `GVL_Param.MAX_AXIS`), `SIZEOF(x)` /
`XSIZEOF(x)` where a library enables them ([stdlib.compat.sizeof]; `x` a
variable declared before it in the same POU, a global or a type), or
`+ - * /` of them; any other bound is error RP0108. An enumeration value as a bound
(`ARRAY[E_Lane.Nr1..E_Lane.Nr10]`, CODESYS and TwinCAT) is its integer value,
with warning RP0135 ([scope.vendor-forms]).

**[variables.located]** `AT` binds a variable to a directly represented
address (`%IX0.0`, `%QW4`, `%I*`, see [lexical.direct-variable]):
`start_btn AT %IX0.0 : BOOL;`. The type must fit the size of the address
([runtime.image.type]); the runtime binds the variable to its place in the
process image ([runtime.image]).

**[variables.initializer]** An initial value is an expression, an array
initializer or a structure initializer:

```
initializer  = expression
             | '[' element { ',' element } ']'                            (* array *)
             | '(' name ':=' initializer { ',' name ':=' initializer } ')' (* structure *)
             | '(' ')'                                                    (* defaults *)
element      = initializer | count '(' [ expression ] ')'                 (* repeated *)
```

In an array initializer `n(v)` stands for `n` elements of value `v`, and
`n()` for `n` elements with their default: `[1, 3(7), 2]` is
`[1, 7, 7, 7, 2]`. IEC 61131-3 writes the count as an integer literal; a constant expression in
parentheses or a call such as `SIZEOF(buffer)` (TwinCAT) is accepted with
warning RP0135 ([scope.vendor-forms]).

A structure initializer may also set the variables of a function-block
instance, `t : TON := (PT := T#1S);` (CODESYS and TwinCAT), and `()` keeps
every default (warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]); IEC 61131-3 leaves out the
initializer).

**[variables.init-arguments]** A function-block instance may be declared
with arguments, `fb : FB_Buffer(size := 10);`, which CODESYS and TwinCAT
pass to the block's `FB_init` method ([pous.oop.fb-init]); the form is
warning RP0119 ([scope.vendor-forms]). Named arguments bind to the inputs of
that name, positional ones to the inputs after `bInitRetains` and
`bInCopyCode`, in order. The arguments are expressions of the declaring POU,
evaluated when its instance is created, just before the FB_init of the
declared instance runs (so `THIS^` is the declaring instance). A block without
`FB_init` takes no arguments (RP0203).

`type_spec` is defined in spec/04-pous.md [pous.type-spec].

## Names and scope

**[variables.unique]** Within one POU, every variable name is declared once,
across all its sections. Names compare case-insensitively
([lexical.identifier.case]). Likewise, every type and POU name is declared once
in a project. A second declaration is error RP0204, reported at the second
one. A user POU may replace a standard function block (spec/08-stdlib.md).

**[variables.resolution]** A name used in a statement or initial value
resolves, in this order, to:

1. a variable of the enclosing POU (in a `FUNCTION`, the function name is
   also the variable holding the result);
2. a global variable ([config.global-list]);
3. a value of an enumeration type, if exactly one enumeration has it
   ([types.derived.enum]);
4. a POU or standard function or function block (spec/08-stdlib.md), when
   the name is called.

A name that resolves to none of these is error RP0203. So is a member that
the structure or function-block instance does not have (`p.z`, `tmr.QQ`).
Members of a function-block or program instance that can be accessed from
outside are its `VAR_INPUT`, `VAR_OUTPUT` and `VAR_IN_OUT` variables.

**[variables.initializer.check]** An initial value must be assignable to the
declared type under the same rules as an assignment (spec/02-types.md). An
array initializer gives the elements in order; a structure initializer names
members of the structure.


======== Specification: spec/04-pous.md ========

# Program organisation units and parsing

*Status: draft v0.1 (syntax). Normative. Diagnostic range RP0200–RP0299.*

This chapter defines the top-level structure of a source file and the general
parsing rules every RootPLC parser follows. Semantics of calls, instances and
Ed3 object orientation follow in a later revision. Grammar notation as in
spec/03-variables.md.

## 1. General parsing rules

**[syntax.lossless]** The syntax tree keeps every byte of the source,
including whitespace, comments and pragmas. Printing the tree gives back the
exact input. Tools that edit code (agents, formatters, migration) therefore
never lose comments.

**[syntax.recovery]** A syntax error does not stop parsing. The parser reports
the error, skips to the next `;` or block keyword (`END_…`, `ELSE`, `ELSIF`,
`UNTIL`, a statement keyword or a new POU) and continues. All syntax errors in
a file are reported in one run, so an agent can fix them together. The
declarations the parser recovers from a file with syntax errors are visible
to the other files; that file's own type errors are reported once its
syntax errors are fixed.

**[syntax.general]** A token that cannot start or continue the expected
construct is error RP0201. The message names what was expected and what was
found.

**[syntax.pragmas]** Pragmas (`{…}`) may appear between any two tokens. The
parser keeps them in the tree but they do not affect the grammar.

## 2. Source file

```
source_file  = { pou }
pou          = program | function | function_block | type_block | test_block
```

**[pous.program]**
```
program      = 'PROGRAM' name { var_section } statement_list 'END_PROGRAM'
```

**[pous.function]**
```
function     = 'FUNCTION' name ':' type_spec { var_section } statement_list 'END_FUNCTION'
``` A function without a
result type (`FUNCTION F` followed directly by its variable sections or body)
is accepted with warning RP0113, because CODESYS and TwinCAT code uses it; it
is called as a statement and has no value (RP0303 when used in an
expression).

**[pous.function-block]**
```
function_block = 'FUNCTION_BLOCK' { modifier } name [ 'EXTENDS' name ] [ 'IMPLEMENTS' name { ',' name } ]
                 { var_section } { member } statement_list { member } 'END_FUNCTION_BLOCK'
member         = method | property
```

Methods and properties may stand before or after the body (IEC 61131-3 puts
them before it, TwinCAT exports them after it). A `;` after a declaration header
(`METHOD M : INT;`) is accepted, as TwinCAT does, with warning RP0134
([scope.vendor-forms]). A PROGRAM may have members too.

## Object orientation

**[pous.action]** An action is a named piece of code of a function block or
program that works on its variables (a CODESYS and TwinCAT extension):

```
action = 'ACTION' name [ ':' ] { var_section } statement_list 'END_ACTION'
```

It behaves like a method without parameters or result: `inst.A()` or, inside
the block, `A()`. Methods, properties and actions written after the end of
their block at the top level of the same file (as CODESYS exports them)
belong to the block before them.

**[pous.namespace]** `NAMESPACE name … END_NAMESPACE` groups declarations and
`USING name;` opens a namespace (IEC 61131-3 ed.3). Declarations inside a
namespace are collected as usual and qualified names resolve by their last
part ([pous.type-spec]); namespace-level name separation is not modelled yet.
Namespaces nest; a global variable may be qualified by any trailing part of
its namespace path (`Lib.Params.x` and `Params.x` for `x` in `Params` inside
`Lib`).

**[pous.oop.class]** `CLASS … END_CLASS` (IEC 61131-3 ed.3) declares a class:
a function block without a body, with variables, methods and properties.

**[pous.oop.modifiers]** `PUBLIC`, `PRIVATE`, `PROTECTED`, `INTERNAL`,
`ABSTRACT`, `FINAL` and, on methods, `OVERRIDE` may precede the name of a
function block, program, function, method or property (some toolchains
write them before METHOD or PROPERTY; that order is accepted too), and an
access modifier may follow `GET` or `SET` of a property. A modifier word is a
modifier only when a name follows it, so `OVERRIDE` may also be a name
([lexical.keywords.soft]). They are accepted and recorded;
access checks and the rules for abstract and final blocks follow in a later
revision.

**[pous.oop.method]** A method is a function that belongs to a function
block or program and runs on one of its instances:

```
method = 'METHOD' { modifier } name [ ':' type_spec ] { var_section } statement_list 'END_METHOD'
```

Its variables are new for every call, like those of a function; the method
name holds the result. Variables in a `VAR_INST` section (CODESYS, TwinCAT; warning RP0134
([scope.vendor-forms])) keep
their value between calls: they belong to the instance, visible only in
that method. Inside the method, the variables of its block
(inherited ones included) are visible by name after the method's own. A
method is called on an instance, `inst.M(args)`, or inside the block or one
of its methods without a prefix, `M(args)`; arguments bind as for functions.
A method without a result type has no value: its call is a statement, and
using it in an expression (`x := inst.M()`) is error RP0303, as for a
function without a result type ([pous.function]).

**[pous.oop.extends]** `FUNCTION_BLOCK B EXTENDS A` makes B a function block
with all variables and methods of A, followed by its own. The base must be a
function block (otherwise RP0111). A variable of B with the name of a
variable of A is RP0204. The body of B replaces the body of A; `SUPER^()`
runs the body of A on the same instance.

**[pous.oop.override]** A method of B with the name of a method of A
overrides it. Every call on an instance runs the method of the instance's own
block, also when the call is made inside a method inherited from A
(`THIS^.M()` or `M()`) or through a reference or pointer of type A
(`p^.M()`): this is dynamic dispatch. `SUPER^.M()` runs A's method without
dispatch. Calling the body through such a reference, `p^()`, likewise runs the
body of the instance's own block (TwinCAT).

**[pous.oop.fb-init]** A method named `FB_init` (CODESYS and TwinCAT) runs
once for every instance of its block when the instance is created, before
the first cycle: instances inside a block before the block, in declaration
order, global variables before program instances. Instances among the local
variables of a function or method are created by every call, so their
`FB_init` runs on every call. Its inputs `bInitRetains`
and `bInCopyCode` are TRUE and FALSE; arguments given in the declaration
fill its other inputs ([variables.init-arguments]). A fault in `FB_init` is reported
by the first cycle. Because the call is implicit, declaring `FB_init` is
warning RP0135 ([scope.vendor-forms]).

**[pous.oop.this]** Inside a function block, program or method, `THIS` is a
reference to the current instance and `SUPER` the same instance seen as its
base block: `THIS^.x`, `THIS^.M()`, `SUPER^.M()`. Through `THIS^` all
variables of the instance are accessible, not only its inputs and outputs.
Elsewhere `THIS` and `SUPER` are RP0203.

**[pous.oop.interface]** An interface declares methods and properties
without bodies:

```
interface = 'INTERFACE' name [ 'EXTENDS' name { ',' name } ] { method | property } 'END_INTERFACE'
```

An interface that extends others has their methods too. An interface name
is a type ([pous.oop.interface-ref]).

**[pous.oop.implements]** `IMPLEMENTS I1, I2` names the interfaces a function
block provides. Every method of each interface, including methods of the
interfaces it extends, must exist in the block or a base block; a missing
method is RP0203. An `ABSTRACT` block is exempt. A name that is not an
interface is RP0111. A block also provides the interfaces of its base.

**[pous.oop.interface-ref]** A variable of an interface type holds a
reference to a function-block instance, or NULL (the initial value).
Assigning or passing an instance of a block that provides the interface
stores a reference to it; an instance of another block is RP0103. `NULL` and
the TwinCAT idiom `0` clear the reference, also as an initial value or a
parameter default; `=` and `<>` compare references
with each other, with `NULL` and with `0`; the `0` is warning RP0127. `itf.M(args)` calls the method of
the referenced instance's own block (dynamic dispatch); through a NULL
reference it is the fault `NULL_REF`. Passing `THIS^` hands out a reference
to the current instance.

**[pous.oop.property]** A property is a value with access methods (a CODESYS
and TwinCAT extension, warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms])):

```
property = 'PROPERTY' { modifier } name ':' type_spec { var_section }
           [ 'GET' { var_section } statement_list 'END_GET' ]
           [ 'SET' { var_section } statement_list 'END_SET' ] 'END_PROPERTY'
```

`PROPERTY`, `GET` and `SET` are not reserved words. Reading a property
(`inst.P`, `THIS^.P`, `itf.P`, or `P` inside the block and its methods)
runs its GET part, in which the property name holds the result. Assigning
it (`inst.P := v`) runs its SET part, in which the property name holds the
assigned value. GET and SET behave like methods: they are inherited, may be
overridden (dynamic dispatch) and may be required by an interface. An
interface property without GET or SET requires a GET part.

**[pous.call.callee]** Only a function, a function block instance, a
program, a method or an action can be called. Calling anything else, for
example a variable of an elementary type (`b(1)` with `b : BOOL`), is error
RP0132. A variable that cannot be called does not hide a function of the
same name: `F(x)` calls the function `F` even where a variable `F` is
visible (OSCAT relies on this).

**[pous.call.in-out]** A `VAR_IN_OUT` parameter refers to the caller's
variable: changes made by the called function or function block are visible
in that variable after the call. RootPLC copies the value in before the call
and back after it. The argument must be a variable, an element or a member
(RP0114); a constant or an expression is an error. A `STRING` or `WSTRING`
parameter holds the caller's whole text, whatever the declared lengths; the
caller's own length applies when the value is written back. While the call runs,
`REF` or `ADR` of the parameter (or of an element or member of it) is the
address of the caller's variable, so it stays valid after the call.

**[pous.call.local-read]** From outside a function block instance or a
program, IEC 61131-3 gives access to its inputs and outputs only. TwinCAT and
CODESYS also let code read its internal variables (`fbPlant.fbMfr.nCount`,
`fbPlant.fbMfr.Receive(x)`); RootPLC accepts such a read with warning RP0130.
Writing an internal variable from outside, also a member or element of it, is
error RP0203, as in TwinCAT. TEST blocks read and write every variable
([tests.whitebox]).

**[pous.call.in-out-constant]** Parameters declared in a `VAR_IN_OUT CONSTANT`
section (CODESYS / TwinCAT; warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms])) are passed like `VAR_IN_OUT` parameters, but the
argument may also be a constant or an expression of any length: RP0114 does
not apply. The
called POU is meant only to read such a parameter; RootPLC does not yet reject
writes to it, and a value argument is not written back.

**[pous.test]** A TEST block is a POU that only the test runner executes
(semantics: spec/07-test-blocks.md):
```
test_block   = 'TEST' name { var_section } statement_list 'END_TEST'
``` `TEST` is reserved only where a test block starts: a POU may be named
`TEST` and `TEST(…)` inside a body is a call (the TcUnit test framework
declares such a function).

**[pous.end]** A POU or block whose closing keyword is missing before the end
of the file is error RP0202. The error is reported at the opening keyword.
CODESYS stores each POU as an object with a declaration part and a body, and
its text exports (one POU per file) leave out `END_PROGRAM`,
`END_FUNCTION_BLOCK` and `END_FUNCTION`. A `PROGRAM`, `FUNCTION_BLOCK` or
`FUNCTION` that reaches the end of its file without its closing keyword, with
no syntax error inside it, is therefore closed there with warning RP0131
instead.

## 3. Types

**[pous.type-block]** Derived types are declared in `TYPE … END_TYPE`. One
block may declare several types, each ended by `;` as in IEC 61131-3; a
missing `;` (CODESYS) is warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]):
```
type_block   = 'TYPE' { type_decl } 'END_TYPE'
type_decl    = name ':' type_spec [ ':=' initializer ] ';'
```

**[pous.type-spec]** Type specifications:
```
type_spec    = elementary [ '[' expression ']' ] [ '(' subrange_or_enum ')' ]   (* STRING[n], INT(0..100), INT (A := 1) *)
             | name                                                         (* derived type *)
             | 'ARRAY' '[' dim { ',' dim } ']' 'OF' type_spec
             | 'REF_TO' type_spec
             | '(' enum_value { ',' enum_value } ')'                         (* enumeration *)
             | 'STRUCT' { var_decl } 'END_STRUCT'
dim          = expression '..' expression | '*'
subrange_or_enum = expression '..' expression | enum_value { ',' enum_value }
enum_value   = name [ ':=' expression ]
```

A type name may be qualified by library namespaces, `Tc2_System.T_MaxString`
or `TcUnit.FB_TestSuite`; RootPLC resolves the last part (library namespaces
are not modelled yet), also in EXTENDS and IMPLEMENTS.

Ed3 object orientation (`CLASS`, `METHOD`, `INTERFACE`, `PROPERTY`) is
reserved for a later revision.


======== Specification: spec/05-statements.md ========

# Statements and expressions

*Status: draft v0.1 (syntax). Normative. Diagnostic range RP0300–RP0399.*

This chapter defines the syntax of statements and expressions. Typing rules
are in spec/02-types.md; evaluation semantics follow in a later revision.
Grammar notation as in spec/03-variables.md.

```
statement_list = { statement }
```

**[statements.terminator]** Every statement ends with `;`, and so does every
variable declaration. A missing `;` is error RP0301, reported at the end of
the statement. After the block statements (`IF`, `CASE`, `FOR`, `WHILE`,
`REPEAT`) IEC 61131-3 also requires the `;` (`END_IF;`); CODESYS and TwinCAT
let it be left out, which is warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]). A lone `;` is an empty
statement.

**[statements.assignment]**
```
assignment   = variable ':=' expression ';'
```

**[statements.assignment.chain]** `a := b := v;` (CODESYS and TwinCAT) means
`b := v; a := b;`; it is accepted with warning RP0125.

**[statements.assignment.set-reset]** The CODESYS and TwinCAT set and reset
assignments `x S= c;` and `x R= c;` mean `IF c THEN x := TRUE; END_IF` and
`IF c THEN x := FALSE; END_IF`; `x` and `c` are `BOOL`. They are accepted
with warning RP0123.

**[statements.call]** A call to a function or function-block instance as a
statement. Arguments are positional, or named with `:=` (input) and `=>`
(output):
```
call_stmt    = variable '(' [ argument { ',' argument } ] ')' ';'
argument     = [ name ( ':=' | '=>' ) ] expression
```
An output binding may leave out the variable, `Done =>`, and an input
binding its value, `bExecute :=` (CODESYS and TwinCAT): the output is not
read, the input keeps its value. A comma may follow the last argument. Both
are warning RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]). A
`REFERENCE TO T` parameter given a variable of type `T` refers to that
variable. Each parameter is given at most once in a call (names compare
without case); binding the same parameter again is error RP0302.

**[statements.if]** `IF c THEN … {ELSIF c THEN …} [ELSE …] END_IF`
evaluates the conditions in order and runs the statements of the first branch
whose condition is `TRUE`, or the `ELSE` branch if none is. Each condition
must be of type `BOOL` (no implicit conversion, spec/02-types.md).

**[statements.case]**
```
case_stmt    = 'CASE' expression 'OF' { case_label { ',' case_label } ':' statement_list }
               [ 'ELSE' statement_list ] 'END_CASE'
case_label   = constant [ '..' constant ]                    (* constant: literal, enumeration value, signed integer *)
```

**[statements.case.timer]** A step chain often times a step with a `TON`
called only in that step's CASE branch. When the branch is left while the
timer's `IN` is still `TRUE`, the timer is no longer called: it keeps
`IN = TRUE` and its start time, so the next time the branch runs it may
fire at once (a homing retried after a timeout faults immediately). Warning
RP0304 is given when a `TON` or `LTON` instance is called only inside the
branches of one CASE statement, and a path through one of those branches
assigns the CASE selector without the timer's last call on that path having
`IN := FALSE` (a literal). No warning is given when the timer is called with
`IN := FALSE` in a branch where it is not started (cleared before
re-entry), or when a branch calls it with `IN := FALSE` and later starts it
(reset before each use). The check is syntactic: it follows IF and CASE
branches but not the values of conditions. To fix, call the timer with
`IN := FALSE` before changing the step, or call it every cycle outside the
CASE with `IN` set to the step condition.

**[statements.for]**
```
for_stmt     = 'FOR' name ':=' expression 'TO' expression [ 'BY' expression ] 'DO' statement_list 'END_FOR'
``` The control variable may also be an array element or a structure member of
integer type (`FOR idx[1] := 0 TO 9 DO`), as TwinCAT accepts, with warning
RP0134 ([scope.vendor-forms]).

**[statements.while]**
```
while_stmt   = 'WHILE' expression 'DO' statement_list 'END_WHILE'
```

**[statements.repeat]**
```
repeat_stmt  = 'REPEAT' statement_list 'UNTIL' expression 'END_REPEAT'
```

**[statements.control]** `EXIT;` leaves the innermost loop. `CONTINUE;`
skips to its next iteration. `RETURN;` leaves the POU.

## Expressions

**[statements.expression.precedence]** Operators, from highest to lowest
precedence. Operators of equal precedence group from left to right.

| Precedence | Operators |
|---|---|
| 1 (highest) | parentheses, function call, `^` dereference, `.` member, `[]` index |
| 2 | unary `-`, unary `+`, `NOT` |
| 3 | `**` |
| 4 | `*`, `/`, `MOD` |
| 5 | `+`, `-` |
| 6 | `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` |
| 7 | `=`, `<>` |
| 8 | `AND`, `&`, `AND_THEN` |
| 9 | `XOR` |
| 10 (lowest) | `OR`, `OR_ELSE` |

Examples:
- `2 + 3 * 4 ** 2` is `2 + (3 * (4 ** 2))`, which is 50.
- `-2 ** 2` is `(-2) ** 2`, which is 4.
- `a + 1 = b` compares `(a + 1)` with `b`.

**[statements.expression.access]** Variables and values:
```
variable     = name { '.' (name | integer) | '[' expression { ',' expression } ']' | '^' }
primary      = literal | variable | variable '(' [arguments] ')' | 'REF' '(' variable ')'
             | '(' expression ')' | 'NULL' | 'TRUE' | 'FALSE'
```
Literals are defined in spec/01-lexical.md.


======== Specification: spec/06-tasks-config.md ========

# Configurations, resources, tasks and global variables

*Status: draft v0.1 (syntax and name rules). Normative. Diagnostics from
RP0200–RP0299 (shared with 03 and 04). The scan-cycle model and task
scheduling follow in a later revision; today `rootplc run` and the test runner
call programs directly.*

Grammar notation: `[x]` optional, `{x}` zero or more, `|` alternative,
`'…'` a literal token.

**[config.global-list]** Global variables are declared in `VAR_GLOBAL`
sections inside a configuration or resource (IEC 61131-3), or outside any
POU as in CODESYS and TwinCAT global variable lists, with warning RP0134
([scope.vendor-forms]):

```
global_list  = 'VAR_GLOBAL' [ 'CONSTANT' | 'RETAIN' | 'NON_RETAIN' ] { var_decl } 'END_VAR'
```

Every global variable is visible in every POU of the project
([variables.resolution]); a variable of the POU with the same name hides it.
Each global name is declared once per namespace (RP0204): two global
variable lists in different namespaces (for example TwinCAT lists, which
are named) may both declare `x`; `GVL_A.x` names one of them, and `x` alone
the one outside any namespace, else the first declared. A `CONSTANT`
global with a constant initial value is a constant: it can be used in array
bounds, string lengths and other constant expressions, and constants may use
the constants declared before them. Global variables keep their values from
cycle to cycle; every TEST block starts with fresh initial values.

**[config.external]** A `VAR_EXTERNAL` section in a POU names global
variables the POU uses. It declares no new variable: the names refer to the
global variables themselves. An unknown name is reported where it is used
(RP0203).

**[config.configuration]** A configuration groups global variables,
resources, tasks and program instances:

```
configuration = 'CONFIGURATION' name { global_list | resource | config_item } 'END_CONFIGURATION'
resource      = 'RESOURCE' name 'ON' name { global_list | config_item } 'END_RESOURCE'
config_item   = task | program_instance
```

A missing `END_CONFIGURATION` or `END_RESOURCE` is error RP0202.

**[config.var-config]** A `VAR_CONFIG … END_VAR` section in a configuration
assigns addresses to variables of program instances by their path
(`Main.fb.start AT %IX0.0 : BOOL;`). It is accepted and recorded; the
addresses are not applied yet.

**[config.task]** A task names a schedule for program instances:

```
task = 'TASK' name [ '(' name ':=' expression { ',' name ':=' expression } ')' ] ';'
```

Typical parameters are `INTERVAL := T#10ms`, `PRIORITY := 1` and
`SINGLE := trigger`. They are recorded but not yet scheduled.

**[config.program-instance]** A program instance runs a PROGRAM, optionally
under a task of the same resource or configuration:

```
program_instance = 'PROGRAM' [ 'RETAIN' | 'NON_RETAIN' ] name [ 'WITH' name ] ':' name
                   [ '(' arguments ')' ] ';'
```

The type must be a PROGRAM declared in the project and the task must be
declared in the same scope; otherwise error RP0203.


======== Specification: spec/07-test-blocks.md ========

# TEST blocks and assertions

*Status: draft v0.3 (assertions, white-box access, runner, mocked time). Normative.*

A `TEST … END_TEST` block ([pous.test]) is a POU that only the test runner
executes. It may declare instances of programs and function blocks, call
them and inspect their inputs and outputs.

**[tests.assert]** The assertion statements are calls of these standard
procedures. A failed assertion fails the test and records the source location.

| Call | Passes when |
|---|---|
| `ASSERT_TRUE(c)` | `c` is `TRUE`; `c` must be `BOOL` |
| `ASSERT_FALSE(c)` | `c` is `FALSE`; `c` must be `BOOL` |
| `ASSERT_EQ(expected, actual)` | the values are equal; both must have a common type |
| `ASSERT_NE(a, b)` | the values differ; both must have a common type |

An argument of the wrong type is error RP0103 ([types.conversion.implicit]).

**[tests.whitebox]** Inside a TEST block, every variable of an instance can
be read and written through `instance.name`, not only its inputs and
outputs. Tests can therefore check internal state. Outside TEST blocks
internal variables can only be read, with warning RP0130
([pous.call.local-read]), except in a white-box adapter ([diff.adapter]).

**[tests.runner]** `rootplc test` runs every TEST block once, on a fresh
machine: variables start with their initial values, the virtual clock starts
at 0. A failed assertion is recorded and execution continues. A run-time
fault (division by zero, index or subrange violation, NULL dereference,
watchdog) ends the test. A test passes when no assertion failed and no fault
occurred.

**[tests.slice]** `rootplc test --slice` compiles only the files the tests
need: every file that contains a TEST block and, repeatedly, every file
that declares a name used in a kept file, as in [diff.slice]. Errors in
other files of the project then do not stop the tests; the command says
how many files it left out. Without `--slice` the whole project must
compile. `--slice` also applies to `--mutate`, where only kept files are
mutated. Use it to test a block inside a project that does not compile
as a whole; the result says nothing about the files left out.

**[tests.time]** Time in a test is virtual. The clock starts at 0 and moves
only when the test calls `ADVANCE(d)` with a duration `d` (`TIME` or
`LTIME`), for example `ADVANCE(T#5s)`. Timers (`TON`, `TOF`, `TP`) read the
clock when they are called, so a typical test calls the instance, advances,
and calls it again. `ADVANCE` is available only in TEST blocks; elsewhere it
is error RP0203. A negative duration does nothing.


**[tests.mutation]** `rootplc test --mutate` measures whether the tests
check the code, not only run it. It makes *mutants*: copies of the project in
which exactly one token is changed by one of these operators:

| Operator | Change |
|---|---|
| comparison | `<` ↔ `<=`, `>` ↔ `>=`, `=` ↔ `<>` |
| arithmetic | binary `+` ↔ `-` |
| logical | `AND` ↔ `OR`, `XOR` → `OR` |
| boolean literal | `TRUE` ↔ `FALSE` |
| negation | `NOT` removed |
| integer literal | `n` → `n + 1` |
| duration | a non-zero value doubled (`T#5s` → `T#10s`; `T#0s` is left alone, doubling cannot change it) |
| enumeration value | `T#V`, `T.V` or `V` → the next value of `T` in declaration order, the last → the first (types declared in the mutated project's files; a bare `V` only when exactly one such type has it). This also mutates CASE labels and state assignments of step chains on enumerations |

Only tokens in statements are mutated: never inside a TEST block, a
declaration section (`VAR` … `END_VAR`, `TYPE` … `END_TYPE`), a comment, a
pragma or a file of a compatibility library ([stdlib.compat]). A `+` or `-`
that follows an operator, an opening parenthesis, a comma, `:=` or a keyword
is unary and is not mutated. With `--mutate-only TEXT`, only files whose
path contains `TEXT` are mutated; the other files still compile and their
tests still run (for example: score a block from a real project with tests
and an adapter kept in other files). Mutants are made in source order; at
most `--mutate-limit N` of them (default 500).

Each mutant is checked and its TEST blocks are run as in [tests.runner]. A
mutant that does not compile is *not viable* and is not counted. A viable
mutant is *killed* when at least one test fails (a failed assertion or a
fault, including the watchdog); otherwise it *survives*. The mutation score
is killed ÷ viable. Mutation needs the unchanged project to compile and pass
every test; otherwise no mutant is run and the command reports why. Each
surviving mutant is reported with its file, line, column, the original token
and its replacement, so a test can be added for it. With `--min-score P`
(0–100) the command fails when the score is below `P` percent.

**[tests.evidence]** `rootplc evidence <file.st|dir>...` writes an *evidence
pack*: one JSON document that records what was verified, so an engineer can
review and sign off a change. Format `rootplc-evidence/0.1`, with:

- `tool`: name and version, and `spec_sha256`, the SHA-256 of the rule set
  compiled into the tool (the spec chapters and the diagnostic registry);
- `inputs`: every source file with its path, size in bytes and SHA-256;
- `libraries`: every bundled library that was active ([stdlib.compat]),
  including the libraries it requires, sorted by name, each with its name,
  version and the SHA-256 of its source files, so a reviewer can repeat the
  verdict with the same library code (for example RootMotion for motion
  programs, [motion.axis]);
- `check`: whether the project compiles, the number of errors and warnings,
  and `iec_clean` (no error and no warning, [scope.vendor-forms]);
- `tests`: each TEST block with its result ([tests.runner]);
- `motion`: every axis a RootMotion axis cycle ran on during the tests
  ([motion.observe]), with its TEST block and variable path, the number of
  axis cycles and hard stops, the peak velocity and acceleration, the
  machine limits, and `within_limits` (the peak velocity is at most
  `MaxVelocity` and, when `MaxAcceleration` is set, the peak acceleration
  is at most `MaxAcceleration`); empty when no axis moved;
- `mutation`: the result of [tests.mutation] (score, killed, viable, each
  survivor), unless `--no-mutate` is given;
- `verdict`: `verified` when the project compiles, has at least one TEST
  block, every test passes, every axis in `motion` is within its limits
  and, with `--min-score P`, the mutation score is
  at least `P` percent; otherwise `not verified`, with `reasons`;
- `signature`: `null`. A pack made by `rootplc` is never signed. A signing
  service may add a signature that covers the pack with `signature` set to
  `null`.

The pack contains no time stamp, so the same inputs and the same tool give
the same pack byte for byte. `--out FILE` writes the pack to a file instead
of standard output; `--markdown` writes a readable summary instead of JSON.
The command fails when the verdict is `not verified`.


======== Specification: spec/08-stdlib.md ========

# Standard library

*Status: draft v0.1 (catalogue for checking). Normative. Exact run-time
behaviour of each block (timing, edge cases) follows in a later revision.*

The names below are predeclared in every project. A user POU with the same
name replaces the standard one.

**[stdlib.fbs]** Standard function blocks. Inputs are set with `:=` in the
call, outputs read as `instance.Q` or bound with `=>`.

| Block | Inputs | Outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `TON`, `TOF`, `TP` | `IN : BOOL`, `PT : TIME` | `Q : BOOL`, `ET : TIME` |
| `R_TRIG`, `F_TRIG` | `CLK : BOOL` | `Q : BOOL` |
| `CTU` | `CU : BOOL`, `R : BOOL`, `PV : INT` | `Q : BOOL`, `CV : INT` |
| `CTD` | `CD : BOOL`, `LD : BOOL`, `PV : INT` | `Q : BOOL`, `CV : INT` |
| `CTUD` | `CU`, `CD`, `R`, `LD : BOOL`, `PV : INT` | `QU`, `QD : BOOL`, `CV : INT` |
| `SR` | `S1 : BOOL`, `R : BOOL` | `Q1 : BOOL` |
| `RS` | `S : BOOL`, `R1 : BOOL` | `Q1 : BOOL` |

**[stdlib.conversions]** Conversion functions ([types.conversion.explicit]):

- `<A>_TO_<B>(x)` for elementary types `A`, `B` (including `STRING` and
  `WSTRING`): `x` must be assignable to `A`; the result has type `B`.
- `TO_<B>(x)`: `x` of any elementary or enumeration type; the result has
  type `B`.
- `TRUNC(x)`: `x` of type `ANY_REAL`; the result is `DINT`, rounded toward zero.

**[stdlib.functions]** Overloaded standard functions. "Common type" means the
type that all arguments convert to implicitly (spec/02-types.md); no common
type is error RP0103.

| Functions | Arguments | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `ABS`, `SQRT`, `LN`, `LOG`, `EXP`, `SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`, `ASIN`, `ACOS`, `ATAN` | one `ANY_NUM` | type of the argument |
| `EXPT(a, b)` | `ANY_REAL`, `ANY_NUM` | type of `a` |
| `MIN`, `MAX`, `MOVE` | values | common type |
| `LIMIT(mn, in, mx)` | values | common type |
| `SEL(g, a, b)` | `BOOL`, values | common type of `a`, `b` |
| `MUX(k, v0, …)` | `ANY_INT`, values | common type of the values |
| `SHL`, `SHR`, `ROL`, `ROR` `(in, n)` | `ANY_BIT`, `ANY_INT` | type of `in` |
| `LEN(s)`, `FIND(s1, s2)` | strings | `INT` |
| `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `MID`, `CONCAT`, `INSERT`, `DELETE`, `REPLACE` | strings, `INT` | `STRING` (or `WSTRING` for `WSTRING` arguments) |

**[stdlib.functions.operators]** The arithmetic and comparison operators
also exist as standard functions with the same meaning: `ADD`, `MUL` (two
or more arguments, `ADD(a, b, c)` is `a + b + c`), `SUB`, `DIV`, `MOD` (two
arguments), and `GT`, `GE`, `EQ`, `LE`, `LT`, `NE` (`GT(a, b, c)` is
`a > b AND b > c`; `NE` takes two). Arguments are positional or `IN1`,
`IN2`, ... in order. A user POU with the same name takes precedence.

**[stdlib.string.length]** The string these functions return is long
enough for any result of its arguments, so nothing is cut before it is
assigned: `CONCAT` returns the sum of the argument lengths, `INSERT` and
`REPLACE` the sum of the lengths of the two strings, and `LEFT`, `RIGHT`,
`MID` and `DELETE` the length of their string, at most 65535 (a string
literal counts with its own length). The target of the assignment keeps
its declared length.

**[stdlib.functions.bounds]** `LOWER_BOUND(arr, n)` and `UPPER_BOUND(arr, n)`
return, as DINT, the lower and upper bound of dimension n (a constant, from
1) of an array. For an array with known bounds they are constants. For an
open array (`ARRAY[*] OF T`, a `VAR_IN_OUT` or `VAR_INPUT` parameter) they
are the bounds of the array passed in, and indexing it checks against those
bounds (fault `INDEX`). A dimension that does not exist is RP0109.

## Compatibility libraries

**[stdlib.compat]** A compatibility library provides the interface of a
vendor library (types, constants, functions, function blocks) in ST, under
the vendor's exact names, so that vendor code checks and runs without edits.
Libraries are bundled with RootPLC and dormant until activated out of band:
`--library NAME` on the command line, the `libraries` argument of the MCP
tools, or a project setting; RootPLC never infers a library from source
text. An active library's declarations join the project like source files
(a user declaration with the same name in the same scope is RP0204; a local
variable hides a library global). A library name may qualify its
declarations: `Tc2_System.PI`. `rootplc libraries` lists the bundled
libraries with their vendor, version and the public references they were
written from (clean-room; RootPLC is not affiliated with the vendors).
Bundled: `Tc2_System` (also `ST_LibVersion`, `F_CmpLibVersion`, the AMS
address types, the task index (RootPLC runs one task, index 1) and
`F_CreateAmsNetId`; the file, ADS and memory functions are declared only) and
`Tc2_Utilities` (TwinCAT; case conversion, trimming, `TIMESTRUCT`, the
`T_Arg` argument helpers `F_INT`, `F_STRING`, ... and `FB_FormatString`,
which formats them like fprintf after the manual's format specification;
the time conversions between `DT`, `TIMESTRUCT` and FILETIME, `LREAL_TO_FMTSTR`,
`LEN2`, `STRNCPY`; the clock, time-zone and ring-buffer blocks are declared only; `Tc2_Utilities`
requires `Tc2_System`, which requires `TwinCAT_BuiltIns`; activating a
library activates what it requires) and
`TwinCAT_BuiltIns` (names every TwinCAT project has: `BIT`, the 64-bit
special types `XINT`, `UXINT`, `XWORD`, `PVOID`, `__SYSTEM.IQueryInterface`,
`__SYSTEM.TYPE_CLASS`, and the system information `_TaskInfo` and `_AppInfo`
of namespace `TwinCAT_SystemInfoVarList`, declared but not filled at run
time)
and `Tc2_Standard` (TwinCAT's `CTU`, `CTD` and `CTUD` with `RESET`, `LOAD`
and `WORD` counts, the `LTIME` timers `LTON`, `LTOF`, `LTP`, and the
`WSTRING` functions `WLEN`, `WMID`, `WCONCAT`, ...) `Tc2_MC2` (the axis interface `AXIS_REF` with its data
types; the PLCopen motion blocks `MC_Power`, `MC_MoveAbsolute`, ... are
declared only, since motion needs the NC) and `Tc3_Module`
(`S_OK` and the other HRESULT constants, `SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`; `HRESULT`
itself, a `DINT`, and `GUID` are in `TwinCAT_BuiltIns`), `Tc3_EventLogger`
(`TcEventSeverity`, `TcEventEntry` and the message, alarm, listener, logger
and text-request blocks with their interfaces, declared only since RootPLC
has no event logger; `FB_TcSourceInfo` is implemented) and `Tc3_JsonXml`
(`FB_JsonSaxWriter` is implemented for objects, arrays, keys, strings,
integers, booleans, null, raw JSON and `DATE_AND_TIME`; its floating-point
and binary methods, the DOM and SAX parsers, the pretty writer, the XML
parser and the symbol-based blocks are declared only). A library may replace a
standard function block of [stdlib.fbs]; while it is active its declaration
is the one used.
Library functions are implemented in ST where their documented behaviour
can be reproduced (for example `BYTE_TO_HEXSTR`).

**[stdlib.compat.pvoid]** `TwinCAT_BuiltIns` makes `PVOID` an untyped
reference: any reference (`ADR(x)`, `REF(x)`, a `REF_TO` variable) converts
to it implicitly, so `MEMCPY(ADR(a), ADR(b), SIZEOF(b))` checks. `Tc2_System`
declares `MEMCPY`, `MEMMOVE`, `MEMSET` and `MEMCMP` with their documented
parameters; they are declared only (RP0120), since RootPLC models addresses
as typed references.

**[stdlib.compat.intrinsics]** `TwinCAT_BuiltIns` also enables `__POUNAME()`,
a STRING constant with the name of the POU it is written in, and `TIME()`,
the time since the PLC started (the virtual clock of the VM).

**[stdlib.compat.dynamic]** `TwinCAT_BuiltIns` enables `__NEW(T)`, which
creates a variable of type `T` (initial values) and returns a reference to
it, `__NEW(T, n)`, which creates `n` elements and returns a reference to the
first, and `__DELETE(p)`, which frees the variable `p` refers to and sets
`p` to NULL; using a reference to a freed variable is the fault `NULL_REF`.
Indexing such a reference as a pointer (`p[i]`) is not supported.

**[stdlib.compat.any]** With `TwinCAT_BuiltIns`, an input of a generic type
(`ANY`, `ANY_NUM`, ...) in a user POU is a `__SYSTEM.AnyType`: `TypeClass`
(`__SYSTEM.TYPE_CLASS`), `pValue` (a reference to the argument; a value that
is not a variable is copied to a new variable) and `diSize` (its size in
bytes, as `SIZEOF`). `pValue` is an untyped reference, so it converts to a
reference of the argument's type; reading it byte by byte (pointer
arithmetic) is not supported. Without the library, generic types in user
declarations stay RP0104.

**[stdlib.compat.query]** `TwinCAT_BuiltIns` enables `__QUERYINTERFACE(src,
itf)`: `src` is an interface reference or a function-block instance; if the
object it refers to implements the interface of the variable `itf`, `itf`
refers to it and the result is TRUE, else `itf` is NULL and the result
FALSE. `__QUERYPOINTER(src, p)` sets the reference `p` to the object
(TRUE) or NULL (FALSE).

**[stdlib.compat.sizeof]** A library may enable compiler operators;
`TwinCAT_BuiltIns` enables `SIZEOF(x)` and `XSIZEOF(x)`: the size in bytes
of a variable or type, a constant, with TwinCAT's 64-bit layout and default
8-byte packing. Elementary types take 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes; `STRING[n]` takes
n + 1 bytes, `WSTRING[n]` 2(n + 1); an array the size of its elements times
their number; references, pointers and interface references 8; an
enumeration the size of its base type (`INT` unless declared). A structure
places each member at an address divisible by its alignment (its size, at
most 8) and is padded to its largest alignment. `SIZEOF`'s result type is
USINT below 256 bytes, UINT below 65536, UDINT below 2^32 and ULINT above;
`XSIZEOF` returns ULINT. The size of a function-block instance (vendor
hidden data) or an open array is not known and is error RP0121. `BIT`
members count one byte each (TwinCAT packs them into shared bytes; this is
not modelled yet).

**[stdlib.compat.declare-only]** A library function RootPLC can declare but
not reproduce faithfully (for example one that copies raw memory) is
declared only. A call is warning RP0120; executing it stops with the
fault `UNSUPPORTED`, so a run never continues with behaviour RootPLC cannot
guarantee. For a declared-only function block this holds for a call of the
block itself, for its methods (also those a derived block inherits and
does not override) and for reading or writing its properties; a library can
also mark a single method as declared only. Declaring instances, passing
them and assigning them to interfaces needs no implementation.

**[stdlib.compat.log]** `Tc2_System`'s `ADSLOGSTR`, `ADSLOGDINT` and
`ADSLOGLREAL` record their message instead of writing to the TwinCAT event
log. The first `%s`, `%d` or `%f` respectively in the format text is replaced
by the argument (a DINT in decimal, an LREAL as `LREAL_TO_STRING` writes it,
which may differ from TwinCAT's number format), and the functions return 0.
`rootplc run` reports each message with the cycle it was written in (from 0)
and its message-type mask (JSON field `log`; text lines `log <cycle>
<mask>: <message>`); a message box (`ADSLOG_MSGTYPE_MSGBOX`) is recorded like
any other message. TEST blocks and `rootplc diff` run the functions without
reporting the messages. The library enables the intrinsic `__ROOTPLC_LOG`
for this; it is not part of any vendor interface.

**[stdlib.compat.unit]** The library `TcUnit` provides the API of TcUnit,
the open-source unit-test framework for TwinCAT 3, written from its public
documentation: `FB_TestSuite` with its assert methods, `TEST`,
`TEST_ORDERED`, `TEST_FINISHED`, `TEST_FINISHED_NAMED`, `IS_TEST_FINISHED`,
`RUN`, `RUN_IN_SEQUENCE` and `TCUNIT_ADSLOGSTR`. Every `FB_TestSuite`
instance registers itself in `FB_init` ([pous.oop.fb-init]); `RUN()` calls
the body of every suite with unfinished tests once per cycle. An assert fails
the current test and keeps the first failure's text; a test named
`DISABLED_...` is skipped. When all suites have finished, each test's result
(suite instance path, test name, passed / failed / skipped, message) is
reported by `rootplc run` (JSON field `tests`). The library enables the
intrinsics `__ROOTPLC_UNIT_RESULT`, `__ROOTPLC_ANY_EQUAL` and
`__ROOTPLC_ANY_TEXT` for this; they are not part of any vendor interface.

**[stdlib.compat.taskinfo]** RootPLC runs one task, index 1. When the
project declares TwinCAT's task information (`_TaskInfo`, library
`TwinCAT_BuiltIns`), `rootplc run` fills task 1 before every cycle:
`CycleTime` is the cycle time in 100 ns units (`--cycle-ms 10` gives
100000), `CycleCount` the number of cycles run before this one and
`FirstCycle` TRUE in the first cycle only and `DcTaskTime` the start of
the cycle on the virtual time of day ([stdlib.compat.clock]) in ns since
2000-01-01 (the EtherCAT distributed-clock epoch). Other members keep their
initial values. TEST blocks drive programs themselves and do not fill it.

**[stdlib.compat.clock]** RootPLC has no wall clock in a run or a test: the
virtual time of day is 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC plus the virtual clock of
the VM (the time since the run or test started, advanced by each cycle or
by `ADVANCE`), so every run is reproducible. `Tc2_System`'s
`F_GetSystemTime` returns it as a Windows file time (100 ns units since
1601-01-01, UTC) and `_TaskInfo[].DcTaskTime` as above. `TwinCAT_BuiltIns`
enables the intrinsic `__ROOTPLC_CLOCK_NS()`, the virtual time of day in
ns since 1970-01-01 UTC as a LINT, for this; it is not part of any vendor
interface.


======== Specification: spec/13-motion.md ========

# Motion: single axis (RootMotion)

RootMotion is RootPLC's bundled motion library, activated like any bundled
library with `--library RootMotion` ([stdlib.compat]). Version 0.1.0 covers
one axis at a time on a **virtual axis**, so motion programs can be tested
and mutation-tested in the VM before anything moves. Real drives (EtherCAT,
CiA 402) use the same blocks later. The function-block names follow the
industry-standard PLCopen motion names. The behaviour below is RootPLC's
definition, written for this toolchain; where it simplifies (for example
homing on a virtual axis), the rule says so.

Safety functions (safe torque off, safe stop) are never part of RootMotion.
They belong to certified safety hardware.

**[motion.axis]** An axis is a variable of type `AXIS_REF`, passed to every
block as `VAR_IN_OUT Axis`. The program sets its configuration before use:
`CycleTime` (seconds per call of `RP_VirtualAxis`, default 0.001),
`MaxVelocity` (units per second, default 1000), `MaxAcceleration` (the
machine's limit in units per second², default 0: no limit set), and the
software limits `LimitsEnabled`, `PositiveLimit` and `NegativeLimit`. The other fields are
state, written only by RootMotion blocks: `State`, `Homed`, `Position`,
`Velocity`, `ErrorID` and internal fields for the active command.

**[motion.cycle]** The program calls the function
`RP_VirtualAxis(Axis := axis)` once per cycle, after the motion blocks of that
axis. It moves the setpoint by one `CycleTime` and returns TRUE while the axis
moves. On a virtual axis the actual position equals the setpoint. A block sees
the effect of the axis cycle at its next call, so a goal reached in cycle *n*
shows as `Done` in cycle *n + 1*.

**[motion.state]** `Axis.State` is one of `MC_AXIS_STATE#Disabled`,
`Standstill`, `Homing`, `DiscreteMotion`, `ContinuousMotion`, `Stopping` and
`ErrorStop`. An axis starts `Disabled`. `MC_Power` moves it between
`Disabled` and `Standstill`. A position move or a halt makes it
`DiscreteMotion`, a velocity move `ContinuousMotion`, a stop `Stopping`. A
software-limit violation makes it `ErrorStop` ([motion.limits]), which only
`MC_Reset` leaves. `MC_ReadStatus` reports the state as one TRUE output.

**[motion.power]** `MC_Power(Enable, Axis)` with `Enable` TRUE makes a
`Disabled` axis `Standstill`. With `Enable` FALSE the axis becomes `Disabled`
at once, its velocity becomes 0, and any active command loses control
([motion.abort]); an axis in `ErrorStop` stays there. `Status` is TRUE while
the axis is neither `Disabled` nor in `ErrorStop`; `Error` and `ErrorID`
report an `ErrorStop`.

**[motion.execute]** Blocks with an `Execute` input start on its rising edge.
Their results (`Done`, `CommandAborted`, `Error` with `ErrorID`) stay TRUE
while `Execute` stays TRUE. When `Execute` is already FALSE as a result
appears, the result shows for one call. A falling edge of `Execute` never
stops a motion that has started. `Busy` is TRUE while the command runs;
`Active` is TRUE while it controls the axis.

**[motion.abort]** A new motion command on an axis takes control from the
command that had it. The older block then reports `CommandAborted` and stops
being `Busy`. The axis continues from its current position and velocity
under the new command, without a jump.

**[motion.errors]** A command that cannot start reports `Error` with
`ErrorID`, and the axis does not change: 1 the axis is `Disabled`, 2 the axis
is in `ErrorStop`, 3 an invalid parameter (velocity, acceleration or
deceleration that is zero or negative where it must be positive, or an
acceleration or deceleration above `Axis.MaxAcceleration` when that is
set), 4 a
software limit was reached, 5 the axis is busy (`Stopping`, or moving where
the command needs `Standstill`).

**[motion.profile]** Position moves follow a trapezoid velocity profile:
the axis accelerates with `Acceleration`, moves at most at `Velocity` (and
never faster than `Axis.MaxVelocity`), and decelerates with `Deceleration` so
that it stops exactly at the target. The velocity never changes by more than
the allowed acceleration or deceleration times `CycleTime` in one cycle,
including the last cycle. Positions are integrated with the average of the
old and new velocity, so a move of distance *s* with peak velocity *v*,
acceleration *a* and deceleration *d* takes *v/(2a) + s/v + v/(2d)* seconds
when *v* is reached (to within one cycle), and the axis ends exactly at the
target.

**[motion.move.absolute]** `MC_MoveAbsolute(Execute, Position, Velocity,
Acceleration, Deceleration, Axis)` moves the axis to `Position`. `Done`
when it has stopped there; the axis is then `Standstill`.

**[motion.move.relative]** `MC_MoveRelative(Execute, Distance, Velocity,
Acceleration, Deceleration, Axis)` moves by `Distance` from the position at
the rising edge of `Execute`, otherwise as [motion.move.absolute].

**[motion.move.velocity]** `MC_MoveVelocity(Execute, Velocity,
Acceleration, Deceleration, Direction, Axis)` brings the axis to `Velocity`
(not negative) in `Direction` (`MC_DIRECTION#Positive` or `Negative`) and
holds it until another command takes control. `InVelocity` is TRUE while the
velocity equals the commanded value; it replaces `Done`.

**[motion.stop]** `MC_Stop(Execute, Deceleration, Axis)` brakes the axis to
velocity 0 with `Deceleration`, aborting the active command. The axis is
`Stopping`, and no other motion command can start until the stop is `Done`
and `Execute` is FALSE; the axis is then `Standstill`.

**[motion.halt]** `MC_Halt(Execute, Deceleration, Axis)` brakes like
`MC_Stop`, but the axis is `DiscreteMotion` while braking, returns to
`Standstill` when it has stopped, and another command may take control at any
time.

**[motion.home]** `MC_Home(Execute, Position, Axis)` needs a powered axis in
`Standstill`. On a virtual axis it sets the position to `Position` at once,
sets `Axis.Homed` and reports `Done` in the same call. (A real drive runs a
homing procedure; the result is the same.)

**[motion.reset]** `MC_Reset(Execute, Axis)` takes an axis out of
`ErrorStop` to `Standstill` and clears `ErrorID`. On an axis without an error
it does nothing but report `Done`.

**[motion.read]** `MC_ReadActualPosition(Enable, Axis)` gives `Position`
while `Enable` is TRUE. `MC_ReadStatus(Enable, Axis)` gives one TRUE output
for the current state ([motion.state]). Both set `Valid` to `Enable`.

**[motion.limits]** With `LimitsEnabled`, a position beyond `PositiveLimit`
or `NegativeLimit` is never reached: the axis stops at the limit, its
velocity becomes 0, it enters `ErrorStop` with `ErrorID` 4, and the active
command reports `Error`.

**[motion.observe]** Every call of `RP_VirtualAxis` reports the axis cycle
to the toolchain: the axis (the path of its variable), the new velocity,
the acceleration of this cycle (the change of velocity divided by
`CycleTime`) and the machine limits `MaxVelocity` and `MaxAcceleration`. A
cycle that ends in a software-limit stop ([motion.limits]) counts as a hard
stop, and its acceleration is not counted. The test runner keeps, for each
TEST block and axis, the number of axis cycles and hard stops, the peak
absolute velocity and the peak absolute acceleration; the evidence pack
reports them ([tests.evidence]). RootMotion enables the intrinsic
`__ROOTPLC_AXIS_CYCLE` for this; it is not part of any vendor interface.


======== Specification: spec/14-runtime.md ========

# Runtime v0: one program on a controller

`rootplc runtime` runs one PROGRAM cyclically on a host: a Linux board for
study case SC1, or a development machine. Version 0 is **demo grade**: it
runs real machines on a bench, but it is not certified and has no fieldbus
yet. It uses the same virtual machine as `rootplc test`, so a program
verified in tests runs unchanged. The runtime sees the program only through
the runtime ABI (`rootplc-abi`): its variables, their addresses and one call
per cycle.

**[runtime.cycle]** The runtime starts the program every `--cycle-ms`
milliseconds (default 10) and runs it to the end once per cycle. Each cycle:
the I/O driver fills the input image, the input image is copied into the
located `%I` variables, the program runs once, the located `%Q` variables
are copied into the output image, and the I/O driver writes the output
image. Time (`TON`, `TIME()`) advances by the real time between cycle
starts. The runtime keeps the number of cycles, the execution time of a
cycle (minimum, average, maximum), the start jitter (how far a cycle starts
from its planned time) and the number of overruns (a cycle that takes longer
than the period; the next cycle then starts at once). On Linux with
PREEMPT_RT, run it under a real-time priority (for example `chrt -f 80`).

**[runtime.image]** The process image has three areas of up to 65,536 bytes
each: inputs (`%I`), outputs (`%Q`) and memory (`%M`). A located variable
([variables.located]) of the selected program, or of a global variable list,
is bound to its address. The number is the **byte offset** in the area
(as in TwinCAT): `%IW2` occupies bytes 2 and 3, `%IX2.0` is bit 0 of byte
