2. The size letter fixes the length and the type: `X` (or none) one bit,
address `byte.bit`; `B` one byte; `W` two bytes; `D` four bytes; `L` eight
bytes. Multi-byte values are little-endian. Memory
variables are copied into the memory image after each cycle and back before
the next, so other image users (for example an HMI) see and set them.

**[runtime.image.type]** In IEC 61131-3 a located variable's type fits
the size letter of its address: `X` takes `BOOL`; `B` takes `BYTE`, `SINT`,
`USINT` or `BOOL`; `W` takes `WORD`, `INT` or `UINT`; `D` takes `DWORD`,
`DINT`, `UDINT` or `REAL`; `L` takes `LWORD`, `LINT`, `ULINT` or `LREAL`.
At a bit address (`X`, or `byte.bit`) another type is error RP0205. At a
`B`, `W`, `D` or `L` address another type is the TwinCAT reading: the
number is the byte offset and the variable's type gives the size
(`x AT %MB20 : REAL` occupies bytes 20 to 23); it is accepted with warning
RP0135 ([scope.vendor-forms]) and the runtime binds the variable's own
size from that byte. A located variable of a type that is not elementary
(a string, array or structure) compiles, but version 0 cannot bind it: the
runtime refuses to start and names it. An address with `*` (`%I*`, not yet
assigned) cannot run either: the runtime refuses to start and names the
variable.

**[runtime.engine]** By default the runtime runs the program in the
virtual machine. With `--engine c` it translates the program to C
([build.c.command]), compiles it to a shared library with the host's C
compiler (`cc`, `gcc` or `clang`, or `ROOTPLC_CC`; on Windows also MSVC)
and runs that instead: the same variables, image binding, retain, status,
Modbus and watchdog, at native speed. The C engine computes what the VM
computes ([build.c.semantics]). It stops at start with a message when the
program uses a construct the C back end does not support, or when no C
compiler is found. Approval-gated deployment ([runtime.deploy]) uses the
VM in version 0.

**[runtime.watchdog]** When a cycle faults (for example a division by zero
or the step budget, [tests.runner]) or its execution takes longer than the
watchdog time (`--watchdog-ms`, default ten periods), the runtime stops the
program, sets every output of the output image to its safe value (all bits
0: every `%Q` BOOL FALSE, every number 0), writes the output image once
more, keeps the memory image, and reports state `fault` with the reason.
The program does not run again until the runtime is restarted.

**[runtime.retain]** With `--retain FILE`, the variables of RETAIN sections
of the selected program and of global variable lists are restored from the
file at start when it exists (a variable whose name or type changed keeps
its initial value and is reported), and saved to it when the runtime stops
and at most once a second while it runs. The file is written to a new name
and then renamed, so a power loss leaves the old or the new file, never a
torn one. Only elementary types are retained in version 0; a structured
RETAIN variable is reported at start and keeps its initial value.

**[runtime.status]** The runtime reports its state (`running`, `stopped` or
`fault`, with the fault), the cycle statistics of [runtime.cycle], and the
values of the program's variables and the located variables, as text or as
JSON (`--json`) when it stops; with `--status FILE` it also writes that
report to the file at most once a second while it runs (written to a new
name and renamed). `--cycles N` stops after N cycles; otherwise the runtime
runs until it is stopped (Ctrl-C).

**[runtime.modbus]** With `--modbus ADDR:PORT` the runtime serves its
process image over Modbus TCP (default address 127.0.0.1; give `0.0.0.0`
to serve the network). Register *n* is bytes 2*n* and 2*n*+1 of an area,
as one little-endian word; bit *n* is bit *n* mod 8 of byte *n* / 8:

| Function | Codes | Range | Area | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coils | 1 | 0– | `%QX` | read |
| Discrete inputs | 2 | 0– | `%IX` | read |
| Holding registers | 3, 6, 16 | 0–32767 | `%M` | read and write |
| Holding registers | 3, 6, 16 | 32768– | `%I` | read; write only while no I/O driver owns the inputs (development, simulation) |
| Input registers | 4 | 0–32767 | `%I` | read |
| Input registers | 4 | 32768– | `%Q` | read |

Writes take effect at the next cycle start. Any other function code, or an
address beyond the image, is answered with the Modbus exception "illegal
function" (1) or "illegal data address" (2). Outputs are written only by the
program, never over Modbus.

**[runtime.deploy]** A running program changes only with a person's
approval. With `--deploy DIR` the runtime accepts new programs through that
directory:

1. `rootplc deploy <files> --to DIR [--program NAME]` checks the project and
   runs its TEST blocks, and writes a deploy request only when it compiles
   and every test passes: the sources and a manifest with each file's
   SHA-256, a SHA-256 over all of them, the program name and the test
   result. The request's code is the first eight hex digits of that hash.
   The command never changes the running program.
2. A person approves the request at the runtime: `rootplc approve DIR`
   shows each pending request (code, program, files, test result) and asks
   for the code, typed at a terminal. It refuses when standard input is not
   a terminal, so an agent cannot approve its own deployment.
3. Within a second, at a cycle boundary, the runtime checks every file
   against the manifest, compiles the program, binds its addresses
   ([runtime.image]), carries over the value of each RETAIN variable that
   has the same name and type in both programs, and runs the new program
   from the next cycle; all other variables start from their initial values
   (a warm start). A request that does not match its hashes, compile or
   bind is rejected and the running program continues. Outputs keep their
   values until the new program writes them.
4. Every request, approval, swap and rejection is appended to
   `DIR/audit.log` with the time, the code and, for an approval, the user
   name of the account that approved it.

The replaced program is kept; `rootplc approve DIR --rollback` turns it into
a new request, approved in the same way. Version 0 relies on the SHA-256 and
the local approval; signed artifacts and authenticated remote approval
follow in runtime v1.


======== Specification: spec/15-blocks.md ========

# RootBlocks: conventions for reusable blocks

RootBlocks is RootPLC's bundled library of typical PLC blocks, organised
in job families (signal conditioning, device modules, sequencing, control,
alarms, modes and states, ...). Applications combine its blocks instead of
writing every job again. This chapter fixes the conventions every block
follows, so blocks combine without glue code and every combination can be
verified the same way. Each block's own behaviour is defined in its block
card (`blocks/cards/`), with numbered rules that its tests check.

**[blocks.library]** RootBlocks is activated like any bundled library,
with `--library RootBlocks` ([stdlib.compat]). Its blocks are named `RB_…`
and written in strict IEC 61131-3 ([scope.iec]). Every block has a card
with: job, interface, behaviour rules, parameters, states and faults,
tests and their mutation score, the blocks it typically combines with, and
what it does not cover. No RootBlocks block is a safety function; safety
functions stay on certified hardware.

**[blocks.command]** A command held for as long as it applies is a level
input (`Enable`, or a device command such as `AutoOpen`); a one-shot
command is an `Execute` input that acts on its rising edge, as in RootMotion
([motion.execute]). A device module has separate automatic and manual
commands, selected by its mode ([blocks.mode]).

**[blocks.mode]** Device modules take `Mode : RB_MODE`: `RB_MODE#Off` (the
device is de-energised), `RB_MODE#Manual` (manual commands apply) or
`RB_MODE#Auto` (automatic commands apply). Interlocks apply in every mode;
manual never bypasses them.

**[blocks.interlock]** `Interlock` TRUE stops or closes the device at once,
in every mode, and keeps it so while TRUE. `Permissive` FALSE prevents a
start but does not stop a device that is already running. Both are inputs
of the block; the logic that computes them belongs to the application.

**[blocks.fault]** A fault latches: the block reports `Error` with a
non-zero `ErrorID` and puts its outputs in the safe state its card defines
(for a device module: de-energised; for a measured value: a substitute
value, such as the last valid one). A rising
edge of `Reset` clears the fault; when the cause is still present, the
fault is detected again. A block never clears its own fault. `ErrorID` 0
means no error; the other values are listed in the block's card.

**[blocks.feedback]** A device module with feedback supervises it: when
the feedback does not match the command for `FeedbackTime` (a parameter),
or two feedback signals contradict each other for that time, the block
faults ([blocks.fault]).

**[blocks.status]** Besides its outputs, a device module reports a status
structure `RB_DEVICE_STATUS` (mode, commanded, active, fault, number of
starts), so an HMI or the runtime's Modbus map can show every device the
same way.

**[blocks.testable]** A block reads time only through the standard timers
and never reads or writes located variables: I/O is mapped by the
application. So every block runs unchanged in TEST blocks, in simulation
and in the runtime ([runtime.image]).


======== Specification: spec/16-diff.md ========

# Differential verification: does a block behave like a reference?

`rootplc diff` runs two function blocks side by side, gives them the same
inputs every cycle and compares their outputs. Uses: checking that a
refactored block still behaves like the old one; checking that a block
from a real project does the job of a catalog block (RootBlocks,
spec/15-blocks.md) and listing where it differs; checking a generated
block against a hand-written one. The answer is evidence from many
sampled cycles, not a proof.

**[diff.command]** `rootplc diff <file.st|dir>... --reference NAME --unit
NAME` loads the sources (with `--library` as for `check`), compiles them,
and compares the function block `--unit` with the function block
`--reference`. Both must be FUNCTION_BLOCKs of the compiled project or of a
loaded library. Options: `--cycles N` (default 1000), `--cycle-ms MS`
(the virtual time per cycle, default 10), `--seed N` (default 1),
`--set NAME=VALUE` (repeatable), `--range NAME=LO..HI` (repeatable),
`--toggle P` (default 0.1), `--tolerance T` (default 0.0001), `--json`.
The exit code is 0 when the blocks agree on every compared output in every
cycle, 1 when they differ, 2 when the comparison cannot run.

**[diff.slice]** Before compiling, `rootplc diff` keeps only the files the
two blocks need: a file that declares the reference or the unit, and,
repeatedly, every file that declares a name used in a kept file (a block,
function, type, interface, namespace or global variable; names compare
case-insensitively; a name used as `Type#Value` counts). The other files
are not compiled, so errors in parts of a project the blocks do not use do
not stop the comparison; the report lists them. Libraries given with
`--library` are always loaded.

**[diff.interface]** The blocks are matched **by name**: an input of the
reference drives the input of the same name of the unit (names compare
case-insensitively), and an output of the reference is compared with the
output of the same name. A real block with other names is wrapped in a
small adapter function block that has the reference's names and calls the
real block; the adapter is ordinary checked code. Inputs or outputs the
other block lacks are listed in the report and not used. Blocks with
`VAR_IN_OUT` cannot be compared (exit code 2).

**[diff.adapter]** Many real blocks keep their I/O as internal variables
(mapped with `AT %I*` in the vendor tool), which an IEC adapter may not
write (RP0203). A function block declared with the pragma
`{attribute 'rootplc.adapter'}` directly before `FUNCTION_BLOCK` is a
*white-box adapter*: in its body and its methods every variable of another
block's instance can be read and written, as in a TEST block
([tests.whitebox]), without RP0130. The declaration itself is warning
RP0136: this is a RootPLC extension for `rootplc diff` and test harnesses,
not portable, and never for code that runs a machine.

**[diff.stimuli]** Before each cycle the virtual clock advances by
`--cycle-ms` and the task information is filled as for `rootplc run`
([stdlib.compat.taskinfo]: cycle time, cycle count, first cycle), then every driven input gets a value from a pseudo-random
sequence that depends only on `--seed`, so a run can be repeated: a BOOL
input changes with probability `--toggle`; an integer or REAL input takes,
with the same probability, a new value spread evenly over its range
(`--range`, default 0 .. 100; integers are whole numbers in the range). An
input given with `--set` keeps that value in every cycle, in both blocks;
a reference input the unit lacks can be set too (for example the reference
block's mode), and is then not reported as missing. Inputs of other
types (TIME, enumerations, strings, structures) keep their initial value
unless they are set. `--set` takes TRUE, FALSE, integers, reals, durations
(`T#1s500ms`) and enumeration values (`TYPE#Value`). Both blocks receive
exactly the same values.

**[diff.compare]** After both blocks have run a cycle, each compared output
is checked: BOOL, integer, enumeration and duration values must be equal;
REAL values may differ by at most `--tolerance`; integer and REAL values are
compared as numbers. A run-time fault in either block (for example a
division by zero) ends the run and is reported with its cycle.

**[diff.report]** The report states the verdict (`agree`, `differ` or
`fault`), the cycles run, the files left out by [diff.slice], the inputs
driven and set, and for each compared
output the number of cycles in which it differed. For the first difference
it gives the cycle, both values, the driven inputs of that cycle and of up
to four cycles before, and the last eight changes of driven inputs before
it with their cycles (timers and supervision often act seconds after the
change that caused them), so the difference can be reproduced as a TEST.
With `--json` the same content is one JSON object.

**[diff.limits]** Both blocks run in one machine and share its global
variables: a block that writes a global variable can disturb the other,
and a block compared with itself may then differ; compare such blocks
through adapters that keep the global state apart, or with TEST blocks.
Agreement means no difference was found in the sampled
cycles; behaviour that the stimuli never reach (a long timer, a rare input
pattern) is not covered. Increase `--cycles`, set slow inputs with `--set`,
narrow ranges with `--range`, or write TEST blocks for such cases.


======== Specification: spec/17-simulation.md ========

# Simulation: scenarios, traces and trace comparison

`rootplc sim` runs one or more programs cycle by cycle on the virtual clock
of the VM, driven by a scenario: values set at given times, expectations
checked at given times or over intervals, and variables recorded in a
trace. A plant model is an ordinary PROGRAM (or a program that calls plant
function blocks) run in the same cycle as the controller, so a controller
and its plant are simulated together without hardware. A recorded trace can
be compared with a later run (regression of the whole behaviour, not only
of assertions). Every run is deterministic: the same sources and scenario
give the same trace.

**[sim.command]** `rootplc sim <file.st|dir>... --scenario FILE` loads the
sources (with `--library` as for `check`), compiles them and runs the
scenario. Options: `--trace FILE` writes the trace ([sim.trace]);
`--compare FILE` compares the run with a trace written earlier
([sim.compare]); `--json`. The exit code is 0 when the run ends without a
fault, every expectation holds and the compared trace (if any) matches; 1
otherwise; 2 when the scenario cannot run (a syntax error in it, an unknown
program or variable, a value that does not fit, or a project that does not
compile).

**[sim.scenario]** A scenario is a text file, one statement per line;
blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored, and so is the rest of
a line after a space followed by `#` (a value cannot contain ` #`);
keywords are case-insensitive:

```
programs PRG_Plant PRG_Main        # run in this order every cycle (required)
cycle T#10ms                       # virtual time per cycle (default T#10ms)
duration T#30s                     # how long to run (required)
record PRG_Main.bRunning GVL_Tank.rLevel
at T#0s set PRG_Main.bStart := TRUE
at T#100ms set PRG_Main.bStart := FALSE
at T#20s expect GVL_Tank.rLevel >= 590.0
from T#1s to T#30s expect GVL_Tank.rLevel <= 900.0
at T#30s expect PRG_Main.bRunning = TRUE
```

- `programs` names the PROGRAMs that form the one simulated task; each is
  instantiated once and they run in the given order in every cycle.
  Global variables are shared.
- `cycle` and `duration` take durations; the number of cycles is
  `duration` ÷ `cycle`, rounded down (at least 1). Cycle `k` (from 0) starts
  at virtual time `k × cycle`.
- `record` (repeatable) adds variables to the trace.
- `at T set PATH := VALUE` writes a value before the first cycle that
  starts at or after `T`. Several `set` lines for the same cycle apply in
  file order.
- `at T expect PATH OP VALUE` checks a value after the first cycle that
  starts at or after `T`; `from T1 to T2 expect PATH OP VALUE` checks it
  after every cycle that starts in `[T1, T2]`. `OP` is `=`, `<>`, `<`,
  `<=`, `>` or `>=`; for REAL and LREAL values `=` and `<>` compare within
  a tolerance given by `within X` at the end of the line (default 0.0001).
  An interval expectation reports its first failing cycle.
- A time after the last cycle refers to the last cycle.

A `PATH` is `Program.variable` with any number of `.member` steps into
function-block instances and structures and `[i]` indices into one-
dimensional arrays, or a global variable (`GVL.name` for a global in a
namespace or global list, or `name`). Names compare case-insensitively.
A `VALUE` is an IEC literal: `TRUE`/`FALSE`, a number, a duration
(`T#2s`), a string in single quotes or an enumeration value `Type#Value`
(the same forms as `rootplc diff --set`, [diff.stimuli]).

**[sim.run]** Before each cycle the VM sets the task information
([stdlib.compat.taskinfo]) and the clock advances by `cycle` after it, as in
`rootplc run`. A fault stops the run; it is reported with its cycle, and the
expectations not yet checked count as not checked (the run fails). The
report lists every expectation with its result (the failing cycle and the
value seen when it fails), the recorded values after the last cycle and the
number of cycles run. With `--json` the report is one object with the fields
`command` ("sim"), `ok`, `cycles`, `fault`, `diagnostics`, `expectations`
(each with `line`, `text`, `ok`, and when it failed `cycle`, `time_ms` and
`value`), `final` (recorded variable → value) and `compare` (null or the
first difference).

**[sim.trace]** A trace is a CSV file: a header `cycle,time_ms,` followed
by the recorded paths as written in the scenario, then one row per cycle
with the cycle number, its start time in ms and each recorded value as IEC
literal text after the cycle. A value containing a comma or a double quote
is quoted as in RFC 4180.

**[sim.compare]** `--compare FILE` reads a trace and compares it with the
run, cycle by cycle, for every path recorded in both. The report gives the
first difference (cycle, time, path, the trace's value and the run's value),
the paths recorded in only one of them, and whether the numbers of cycles
differ. REAL and LREAL values compare within 0.0001 (relative to the larger
magnitude when it exceeds 1). A recorded trace and an unchanged project
always compare equal.

**[sim.limits]** v0 runs one task (no task priorities or intervals per
program), has no FMI plants or simulated fieldbus devices (spec Phase 2,
G2) and records values after each cycle only.


======== Specification: spec/18-codegen-c.md ========

# Native code: Structured Text to C

`rootplc build --target c` translates a checked project into one portable
C99 file. The C code computes what the VM computes: the same values after
every cycle and the same faults. It is the path to native execution on a
controller, to MCU targets through the C runtime shim and to model checking
with CBMC (spec Phase 2). The VM stays the reference: the C back end is
checked by running the same programs both ways and comparing every variable
after every cycle.

**[build.c.command]** `rootplc build <file.st|dir>... --target c --out DIR`
loads the sources (with `--library` as for `check`), compiles them and
writes `DIR/rootplc_program.c`. `--program NAME` chooses the PROGRAM when
the project has several. The exit code is 0 when the file was written, 1
when the project does not compile, 2 when the program uses a construct the
C back end does not support yet ([build.c.subset]); the report names the
first such construct and its location. `--json` gives one object with the
fields `command` ("build"), `ok`, `target` ("c"), `program`, `out`,
`diagnostics` and `unsupported` (null or `{file, line, column, construct}`).

**[build.c.file]** The file is self-contained: it includes only the C
standard headers `stdint.h`, `string.h`, `math.h`, `setjmp.h` and, for the
main function, `stdio.h` and `stdlib.h`. It defines one C structure per
structure type, function block and program (members in declaration order,
named `v_` followed by the declared name), a body function per POU, and
three entry points:

- `void rootplc_init(void)` sets every variable to its initial value;
- `int rootplc_cycle(int64_t cycle_ns)` runs one cycle of the program
  and then advances the clock by `cycle_ns`; it returns 0, or the fault
  code ([build.c.faults]) when the cycle stopped with a fault;
- `int64_t rootplc_now_ns` is the clock read by timers and `TIME()`.

Compiled with `-DROOTPLC_MAIN`, the file also has a `main(argc, argv)`:
`program CYCLES CYCLE_MS` runs that many cycles and prints every
elementary variable of the program, one per line, as `name=value`
(`TRUE`/`FALSE`; integers, durations and dates as decimal integers in
their units; REAL with `%.9g` and LREAL with `%.17g`, which read back
exactly; strings in UTF-8 with `$` written `$$` and control characters
as `$N`, `$R`, `$T` or `$hh`), then `cycles=N`, and `fault=KIND` when a cycle stopped with a
fault (exit code 1).

**[build.c.semantics]** The generated code follows the VM (spec/02-types.md,
spec/05-statements.md, [stdlib.fbs]): integer results wrap to their type (two's
complement), REAL arithmetic is computed in double precision and rounded to
single precision, real-to-integer conversion rounds half away from zero and
saturates (NaN gives 0), FOR evaluates its end and step once and stores the
next value with the control variable's type, CASE takes the first branch
whose labels contain the value, function inputs that are not given take
their initial value, and the standard function blocks keep the same state
as in the VM. Timers read `rootplc_now_ns`. Arguments of a call are
evaluated left to right in the VM; in C their order is unspecified, so a
call whose arguments have side effects on each other may differ.

**[build.c.faults]** Division or modulo by zero (`DIV_BY_ZERO`, code 1),
an array index outside its bounds (`INDEX`, code 2), a value outside a
subrange (`RANGE`, code 3) and dereferencing NULL (`NULL_REF`, code 4)
stop the cycle as in the VM. The statement limit
of the VM (`WATCHDOG`) is not modelled; a runtime uses its own watchdog.

**[build.c.strings]** STRING and WSTRING values are sequences of
characters (Unicode code points), as in the VM: lengths, positions and
truncation count characters. Every string is stored with the capacity of
the longest string the program declares or writes (at least 16), and a
value stored in a `STRING[n]` is cut to `n` characters. The string
functions LEN, FIND, CONCAT, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, INSERT, DELETE and REPLACE,
comparisons (character by character), conversions from a string to an
integer (the number the text spells, else 0) or a CHAR (its first
character), and conversions to a string from integers, BOOL, CHAR, TIME
and LTIME are supported. Not yet: REAL, dates, times of day and
enumerations as text, and character access `s[i]`.

**[build.c.subset]** v0 supports: elementary types, strings
([build.c.strings]), enumerations, subranges, aliases, arrays with fixed bounds, structures;
programs, functions (inputs and outputs) and function blocks (inputs,
outputs, locals, nested instances); global variables; every statement;
the operators; the standard function blocks TON, TOF, TP, R_TRIG, F_TRIG,
CTU, CTD, CTUD, SR and RS; the standard functions ABS, SQRT, LN, LOG, EXP,
SIN, COS, TAN, ASIN, ACOS, ATAN, EXPT, TRUNC, MIN, MAX, LIMIT, SEL, MUX,
MOVE, SHL, SHR, ROL, ROR, the type conversions between elementary types
and `TIME()`; references (`REF_TO`, `REF()`, `^`, NULL, comparisons for
equality; C pointers) and VAR_IN_OUT parameters of functions and function
blocks, copied in before the call and back after it as in the VM
([pous.call.in-out]); the object-oriented features ([build.c.oop]).
Only the global variables the program uses are emitted, and those with an
address or in a RETAIN section. Not yet: `REF()` of a VAR_IN_OUT parameter
(the VM reaches the caller's variable), indexing a reference `p[i]`,
`__NEW`, VAR_STAT, UNION, compatibility-library intrinsics and TEST blocks
(tests run in the VM).

**[build.c.oop]** Methods, properties and actions run in a frame of their
own with a pointer to the instance (`THIS`). Every function-block and
program instance carries the number of its block as a hidden first member,
and a derived block's structure begins with its base block's members, so a
pointer to a derived instance is also a pointer to its base. A method
called with dispatch ([pous.oop.override]), a method called through an
interface ([pous.oop.interface-ref]) and a block body called through a
reference run the method or body of the instance's own block, chosen by
that number among the blocks the program uses; `SUPER^.M()` runs the named
method itself. An interface value is a pointer to the instance; calling a
method through NULL is the fault `NULL_REF`. At start-up, and for the
instances among the local variables of a function or method on each call,
FB_init runs inner instances first with `bInitRetains` TRUE, `bInCopyCode`
FALSE and the declaration's arguments ([pous.oop.fb-init],
[variables.init-arguments]); a fault in it is reported by the first cycle.
An instance may have an initial value for its inputs (`fb : FB_X := (in :=
5)`).

**[build.c.abi]** For a runtime the file also defines (non-static, and
exported from a shared library when compiled with `-DROOTPLC_SHARED`):

- `rootplc_vars` and `rootplc_nvars`: the variable table of the runtime ABI
  (spec/14-runtime.md), the program's variables then the global variables
  emitted, each with its name, kind (0 other, 1 BOOL, 2 signed integer,
  3 unsigned integer or bit string, 4 REAL, 5 LREAL), size in bytes, type
  name, direct address text (`%IX0.0`, or NULL), RETAIN flag and a pointer
  to its storage (a BOOL is one byte, 0 or 1; numbers in the C types of
  [build.c.file]);
- `int rootplc_step(int64_t elapsed_ns)`: advance the clock by the time
  since the previous cycle started (0 for the first), then run one cycle;
  it returns 0 or the fault code, like the VM engine's cycle;
- `uint32_t rootplc_abi_version(void)`, the ABI version (0).

Located and RETAIN variables are ordinary storage in the C file: binding
them to the process image and keeping them is the runtime's job.

**[build.c.shim]** `runtime-c/` is a C99 runtime for the generated file,
for targets without a Rust runtime: `rootplc_rt.c` binds the located
variables of the table to a process image ([runtime.image]: inputs,
outputs and memory, byte offsets, little-endian, the variable's own size at
a byte address), and `rootplc_rt_cycle` copies inputs in, steps the
program and copies outputs and memory out; after a fault it sets the output
image to 0 (safe outputs, [runtime.watchdog]) and the program stops. A port
supplies the clock, the sleep until the next cycle and the I/O;
`ports/posix` runs cyclically on Linux (and other POSIX systems) with the
image kept in memory.


======== Specification: spec/19-lsp.md ========

# Editor support: the language server

`rootplc lsp` is a Language Server Protocol server on stdio, so editors
(VS Code, Neovim, Emacs, JetBrains, Zed …) show RootPLC's diagnostics while
a person types, with hover, go-to-definition and an outline. It is the
human side of the same checks agents get through `rootplc check` and MCP:
the diagnostics, codes and hints are identical.

**[lsp.transport]** Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 framed with a
`Content-Length` header, as the LSP specification defines. The server
answers `initialize` with its capabilities (full text synchronisation,
hover, definition, document symbols), handles `initialized`, `shutdown`
and `exit`, and ignores notifications it does not know. A request it does
not know gets the error `MethodNotFound` (-32601). Positions are 0-based
lines and characters; RootPLC counts characters in code points.

**[lsp.project]** The project is every `.st` file under the workspace
folder given in `initialize` (`rootUri` or the first `workspaceFolders`
entry) plus documents the editor opened outside it. An open document's
text in the editor replaces the file on disk. `initializationOptions` may
give `{"libraries": ["Tc2_System", ...]}` to activate compatibility
libraries, as `--library` does.

**[lsp.diagnostics]** After `didOpen`, `didChange` and `didSave` the
server checks the project and sends `textDocument/publishDiagnostics` for
every project file that has diagnostics, and an empty list for a file whose
diagnostics went away. Each diagnostic has the range of the rootplc
diagnostic, its severity (error 1, warning 2), its code (`RPnnnn`), the
source `rootplc` and the message, followed by the hint when there is one.

**[lsp.symbols]** `textDocument/documentSymbol` lists the declarations of
the document: programs, function blocks, functions, methods, interfaces,
types, TEST blocks and global variable lists, each with the variables it
declares as children. It works on text that does not compile.

**[lsp.definition]** `textDocument/definition` on a name finds its
declaration: a variable of the enclosing POU (or the global variables),
then a POU, type, method or global variable anywhere in the project. Names
compare case-insensitively.

**[lsp.hover]** `textDocument/hover` on a position inside a diagnostic's
range shows the explanation of its code (the text of `rootplc explain`);
on a declared name it shows the declaration's line.
